#114877. Industry News: An Unimaginable Tragedy Took Her Children. They’re the Reason She Keeps Running—No Matter How Much It Hurts.

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 20m • 📚 Deep Dive (3996 w)
📖 Baca

Industry News: An Unimaginable Tragedy Took Her Children. They’re the Reason She Keeps Running—No Matter How Much It Hurts.

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3996 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that there are moments on the trail when Karen Sparks stops running.
  • Karen took up running in the years after she lost her world.
  • Erwin Park rises rather unexpectedly out of ranchland and rolling prairie where longhorn cattle dot the landscape.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story was originally published in June 2021.

It has been revealed that there are moments on the trail when Karen Sparks stops running. She puts her hands to her knees, opens her mouth, and lets the sound that’s been building find release. The noise starts low and feral, then rises from the depths, growing sharp and loud enough to echo under the canopy of oaks where she runs each day. Karen doesn’t care who hears it. The sound fuels her.

Karen took up running in the years after she lost her world. She liked the feel of her feet pounding the earth; the shock and adrenaline needed somewhere to go. But it wasn’t until she discovered this wooded trail in Erwin Park in McKinney, Texas, that she felt something close to peace. Nature is her church. She was raised Baptist but can no longer bring herself to enter a church. She’s been angry with God.

Erwin Park rises rather unexpectedly out of ranchland and rolling prairie where longhorn cattle dot the landscape. Tucked away inside the trees, Karen feels protected. She talks to her kids. She talks to herself. She runs along the dry-cracked mud, next to riverbeds and over trees fallen in the path.

Karen strained her piriformis, a buttock muscle, when she was younger. She’s 43 now, and sometimes when she’s running her hamstrings get so tight it feels like her muscles might rip. Maybe she likes being in pain, or maybe she likes knowing that the pain does not own her. Anyway, she’s in pain all the time. Spiritually, emotionally, physically. When it gets bad, she tries talking to her body. I’m grateful for this hamstring, she claims. I’m grateful for this pain. She thinks about people who can’t do this. Because they’re in a wheelchair or in a hospital bed, or because they’re not here anymore.

She thinks about Reagan and Grant.

On the fifth anniversary of their death, November 1, 2015, she ran a hundred miles on the nine-mile loop in Erwin Park. She’d originally signed up for the Indiana Trail 100, but the pandemic brought an end to that strategy, and Karen could not be deterred. So she created her own race, an ultramarathon for one. People told her she was crazy, and maybe she was. But she’d spent previous anniversaries hiding from the world, walloped by grief, and this year she was flipping the script on the tragedy that had come to define her life.

The trail was steep and winding. After sunset, the moon lit her path. Each time she thought about quitting, her mind flashed to the man who took her children. Each step was vengeance. Her feet pounded and pounded, like she could pound him into the ground.

Recent findings suggest that on the day her children died, Karen could not move. She remembers falling to the floor in the living room of her parents’ house, curling her body around a framed picture of Reagan and Grant that she clutched to her chest. A neighbor had phoned to say the home she once shared with the man she no longer called her husband was burning, and she dialed her father, who was on his way to pick up the kids.

He’s killing my kids, she said, and she kept repeating the words, because some dark force had overtaken her, and it’s like she knew. Dad, hurry. He’s killing them.

It has been revealed that her father dashed to the scene, where he found firefighters and a home lapped by flames. Karen stayed frozen, and she still gets angry when she thinks of this detail. Why didn’t she go to them? Why didn’t she race to her car and drive 190 miles an hour to reach them? She can’t explain. She only kept rocking back and forth, back and forth. The next thing she remembers is her uncle walking through the front door. He kneeled beside her and whispered in her ear, “They’re gone.”.

Industry observers note that it was her best friend, Brandy, who got her running. Brandy was once a lost teenager who shot up heroin; now she’d become a sober woman who found release through her body in motion, and she wanted Karen to find it too.

It has been revealed that she did, but often it felt like anguish. She muttered and cussed and yelled. This is stupid. It hurts. Why am I doing this? Karen didn’t like running so much as she needed running. She needed the catharsis, the endurance challenge. She wanted to suffer. She ran a half marathon less than a year after the tragedy, a full marathon the next.

Still, the grief escalated. The shock and adrenaline wore off after two years, leaving a fathomless despair. One night in May 2018, she laid out hydrocodone, Valium, and Xanax. The proposal was to wash them down with vodka and wine and not wake up.

Her memory of that night is spotty, but she remembers looking at a picture of Reagan and Grant. She was desperate, sobbing. She did not want to die, but she could not understand what she was doing on Earth without them. I need you to intervene, she begged them. Soon after, she remembers getting a text from a cousin checking in on her, then another cousin, then a friend, then her sister. Karen took it as a sign. She threw away the pills.

Two weeks later, her father checked her into a residential treatment center outside Nashville that specialized in trauma. It was a serene place, acres of rolling pasture, and Karen spent hours on the wooded trail out back, running. Some people who lose their children don’t make it. Alcohol and drugs take them; the suicide rate is higher than average. Eventually Karen came to accept that if she died, then Reagan and Grant died with her, and she couldn’t let them die twice.

Recent findings suggest that she discovered the trail at Erwin Park after returning home to North Texas. Over the next two years her race distances ramped up promptly, from 50 miles to 100K. Karen, who had once made fun of Brandy’s cracked and blistered feet, was now the one peeling off toenails, running her fingers over the watery bubble of a blister. The fifth anniversary of her children’s death was the first time she ran 100 miles. As the hours went by, she checked her watch, trying to place each of her children’s last moments. This is when he was pouring the gas, this is when he texted.

She could feel Reagan and Grant on that trail. She always does. A cardinal fluttering past, a heart shape in the stumps of the trees, a pair of blue jays—they’re reminders that although she lost her children, they are with her still. Reagan and Grant are the reasons to keep going—not just over the 100 miles, but in the life she is still figuring out how to live.

In a recent development, karen Sparks had a different life once. She was 25 when she met David Small at the mortgage manufacturer where they worked. A clean, good-looking man, a real charmer. He was eight years older. She liked the salt-and-pepper hair, the goatee. She was wearing pink corduroy pants and a floral top that day; he complimented the outfit. Karen needed compliments. Ever since adolescence—the glasses, the braces—she’d struggled with a sense that she was not pretty enough, not thin enough. Not enough.

In a recent development, karen already had a boyfriend and kept a photo of him at her desk. “He won’t be that for long,” David told her. “I’ll have you.” She laughed, because obviously that was a joke. A bit arrogant, too, though she liked the feeling of being coveted. He was smirking, a micro-movement that struck her then as benign.

According to recent reports, to understand why Karen fell so hard for David Small, it helps to understand how badly she wanted to escape. Garden-variety teenage rebellion had escalated fast. She’d been a cheerleader and athlete, the daughter of a charismatic high school football coach who became the principal, but in her 20s, she watched Brandy rope off her arm with a rubber tube and plunge a needle into a vein. Around that time, Karen was arrested for drunk driving. She knew she needed to find a better path.

Recent findings suggest that and she did, but she didn’t. She traded the nice boyfriend for the charming bad boy at the office. She’d dropped out of college, which was probably a mistake, and the working world had been a series of dull cubicle gigs. More than anything, she wanted a family. She wanted to be a wife and a stay-at-home mother. Motherhood felt like a purpose. She’d never been a star student or athlete, but she had heart. She was the kid on the team who got the “hardest worker” award. And maybe because her own father had been so powerful, she believed that marrying David could give her those things.

It has been revealed that her mother didn’t like the guy, but Karen’s father urged his wife to give him the benefit of the doubt. Duke Sparks is a Santa Claus of a man, substantial laugh, big smile. The eldest of 10, with an alcoholic dad, he raised his siblings. Maybe his mistake—he thinks about this all the time—is that he couldn’t stop saving his daughter. Whatever she wanted, he gave it to her, so when she fell for this man, he wasn’t going to stand in her way. When she asked for the fairy-tale wedding, he gave it to her, even though $30,000 was a chunk of change for a school administrator and his schoolteacher wife.

Industry observers note that she bought the gown at one of those substantial bridal warehouses. Silver-ivory beads embroidered on the straight corset, a long flowy bottom like a princess at a ball. She took bridal photos in front of black-eyed Susans at a Dallas park that was popular with brides-to-be. She sits on the lawn with a tiara nestled in her brown beachy waves, the diamond ring with three bands fitting together like interlocking puzzle pieces conspicuous on her finger as she rests her cheek in her palm. Karen doesn’t recognize the 27-year-old woman in that picture. It’s like she’s wearing a mask.

The newlyweds moved to a one-story in McKinney, about a half hour north of Dallas, and then a two-story a little farther north in the small town of Van Alstyne. In 2006 she had a baby girl named Reagan, and 17 months later a baby boy named Grant, and the way those two came into the world was the way they walked through it: Reagan swift and bold, Grant taking his time, circumspect. Reagan was Karen’s mini-me. The girl of a thousand smiles, with a smattering of freckles. She was a gymnast who loved to climb the walls, climb the refrigerator, climb anything. The summer before the fire, Reagan learned the backstroke and Grant had just gotten comfortable in the pool. Out on the field, though, he was a heck of a ballplayer. He was very particular about his clothes—everything had to match—and had a thing for neons. Those two loved tricking their grandfather into eating Sour Patch Kids. They’d promise him the candy wasn’t sour—definitely not sour, no way was it sour—then when he popped one into his mouth and his face puckered, they’d fall to the floor laughing. They were happy kids. The marriage was rocky, surely they heard things, but Karen is pretty sure they were happy.

Industry observers note that david had trouble keeping a job, though. He had trouble keeping the electricity on, keeping the mortgage paid. In a word, he had trouble. He pawned her ring shortly after Grant was born. Karen sat on the steps of their lease-to-own home, weeping. How could this happen? We have to make sacrifices, that’s what he said. He promised it would never happen again, but it just kept happening. Karen’s credit card started getting declined. David once bought the kids scooters for Christmas, only to pawn them. He kept the car parked in the back to keep it from repo men.

It has been revealed that after the fire, Karen visited the house. She had to retrace the steps, witness the damage with her own eyes. She pulled back the canvas that investigators had draped over the carpet in the master bathroom. She had to see it: The silhouettes of her children’s bodies, soot outlining their final positions like sidewalk chalk. Some mothers never want to go back, she gets it, but she needed this. What also stands out from that visit is the enormous engagement photo of her in that wedding dress. Flames had licked the canvas, so the picture-perfect image had crackled and turned blister-black.

Industry observers note that why did you stay? Karen could torture herself with this until the end of time if she wanted to. Did you ever think he was capable of such wickedness? Of course not! He never hit her. He never hit the children, never even threatened it. No drinking problem, no drug addiction, no gambling, as far as she can tell. But when Karen scans for warning signs, she thinks about his charm. The subtle manipulation, gaslighting, coercion. How many serial killers, how many con men, how many two-bit criminals get described this way by some innocent bystander? He was so nice, so good-looking, so charming. David’s favorite movies were The Talented Mister Ripley and Catch Me if You Can. So yeah, that was a clue.

In a recent development, some signs were more obvious, especially to people who weren’t Karen. Her sister trailed him twice to see if he was going to work. (He wasn’t.) Though their memories of the incident are foggy, Karen remembers that her sister tried to show her a photo of him meeting another woman. Karen couldn’t hear it. David loved her. He loved their kids. Karen had gone on antidepressants for postpartum depression after Grant was born, and she wonders if the meds kept her hazy.

According to recent reports, also, Karen did not quit things. The little girl who got “hardest worker” trophies would not give up on her marriage so easily. Resilience would be her strength, and her undoing.

It was her father who finally convinced her to leave. Duke had run a background check and found David had an outstanding arrest warrant for unpaid traffic tickets. He called his daughter from the football field. He’s driving around with your kids, he told her. If they arrest him, they’re taking those kids to social services.

In a recent development, that startled Karen. Reagan was 9. Grant was 8. Her instinct to protect them overrode any fear of leaving.

She pulled David into the bathroom one night so they could talk in private. The bathroom had a worn brown carpet that led to a walk-in closet. She leaned against the countertop with the double sink and spoke in a voice more defeated than angry. This was over. No fighting. His voice was calm, too. I’m sorry, baby. I’ll fix it, baby.

According to recent reports, the fire began in the garage. He’d poured gasoline through the house, dousing the walls, dousing the furniture. The investigators had never seen so much gas. The children lay on the carpet inside the master bathroom where he and Karen had stood just a month before, when she’d told him it was over.

Sources indicate that how he kept the kids compliant is a mystery. No drugs were found in their system, no sign of struggle. The children were arranged the way they usually slept, Reagan on her side, Grant on his tummy. David’s body was curled in a ball at the back of the closet, holding down one of the dogs. That sorry coward had placed his kids closest to the flame.

In a recent development, karen had finally left him on October 19. Her attorney had recommended that she go without warning, so she moved the kids to her parents’ place. After David was served divorce papers, he told her he didn’t see it coming. He just didn’t think his wife would do this.

“You got me,” he texted her that day.

She shot back, “I learn from the best.”.

Sources indicate that halloween had been his first weekend alone with the kids. Karen saw no reason to punish him, even though he seemed to be punishing her. He took Reagan and Grant trick-or-treating, but he didn’t send one photo to Karen of them in their costumes.

Then came Sunday, November 1, 2015. He started texting her at 6 a.m. Are you coming to church with us?

According to recent reports, was he kidding? No, she wasn’t going to church with them. She wasn’t playing “happy family” anymore.

The texts kept coming, all morning long. I need to talk to you. There’s something I need to tell you. Her family told her to ignore him. Do not go back, it’s a trap. Karen had gone back so many times. She stayed firm. The texts stopped around noon.

Recent findings suggest that her mind runs alternate scenarios of what might have happened if she’d gone that day, and though she’ll never know, she believes he would have killed her. She thinks he wanted to take them all down together. Instead, he took her children, the pets, most of her belongings, her unshakable faith in God, nearly everything she had, and left her the lone survivor.

It has been revealed that from what Karen can piece together, it seems his initiative was to blow up the house, leaving nothing but ashes. But the trail of fire never reached the master bathroom. The bodies did not burn. Cause of death, carbon monoxide poisoning and smoke inhalation. Karen hates the phrase “at least”—at least you got them for nine years, at least you were a mother for a while—but this part really is an at least. He’d left a suicide note. Some nonsense about seeing her in heaven. How long had he been plotting this? Some answers she’ll never get.

Was he unstable? Clearly. Narcissistic sociopath turned psychopath, that’s her best guess. Karen has spent the past five-plus years puzzling out the question of why, and she hasn’t gotten far. Part of her trauma therapy at the treatment center was reenacting that day, placing herself in the scene she never entered in real life, a technique known as psychodrama. The benefit was profound, but it never gave her the “why.” There is no word in the English language for a mother who loses her children, the way there is for widows and orphans. It’s like language itself cannot admit the possibility.

The fourth year was even harder than the first three. Grief kept amplifying. She got tattoos. Their names on her outer left forearm. Their birth dates in Roman numerals on her inner right wrist. Angel wings on her ankles, which she got with another mother who’d lost her kids. And on the tender ivory of her inner bicep, the phrase that has become her motto: Love never ends. She dyed her hair magenta and started painting her nails in bright neons. The look is a bit out there for a 43-year-old woman in small-town Texas, but the wildness fits her soul, and she likes to think her kids are proud. She believes they see her the same way she sees them.

Sources indicate that on November 1, 2020, Karen ran the 100 miles by herself, but she wasn’t alone. People had flocked to support her. One woman ran alongside her for 50 miles. Another flew in from Indiana to crew. Karen didn’t even know some of these people. But they had heard her story and wanted to help. At pit stops, her coach and his wife massaged her feet. It felt nearly Biblical. Her feet. Her dad was there from beginning to end, sleeping in his truck at night.

In a recent development, karen had never seen a pit crew hustle so hard; it felt like NASCAR. They changed her clothes, popped her blisters, fed her when her stomach could take it. Pringles, PB&J sandwiches, ice-cold Coca-Cola. Her favorite was mashed potatoes and ramen. Sounds disgusting, but it went down smooth and easy as night fell.

Somewhere in the dark, she started to hallucinate. The trees came alive. They turned into fairyland creatures, with swooping limbs and kind faces. Karen was Little Red Riding Hood, running from the Significant Bad Wolf. She was Katniss Everdeen, an ordinary girl who never asked to be a hero. The sun came up, she scarfed down pancakes and syrup, and she could see the faces of the people who demonstrated up for her, and the feeling was golden.

Around mile 70, she started to crumble. She broke down when she briefly couldn’t find her dad at the pit stop. Duke wondered if it was time for his daughter to call it quits, but he knew her better than that. She would crawl to the end if she had to, but she would finish.

It has been revealed that it took Karen 31 hours to complete the run, an hour longer than planned. She beat herself up about the extra time until her team reminded her that what she’d done was harder than most races, not just because of the personal stakes but because she couldn’t feed off the energy of other runners, spectators, all those passing people. Even Karen had to admit: One woman, 100 miles. It was a triumph.

Karen had never wanted this. She only wanted to be a mom. But this loss summoned a strength she didn’t know she had. Back in her previous life, she did not have the courage to stand on her own. This part is confusing, it fills her eyes with tears, because losing Reagan and Grant was the worst thing that had ever happened to her—but it also made her more like the woman she wanted to be.

She’s working on a memoir with her sister, and she plans to keep racing. Another 100-miler in October, a 200-miler after that; her dream is the Moab 240. Reminders of her loss never go away. Kids playing on a jungle gym. An empty swing. The memories can bring a smile, or they can bring a tear. She has learned to live with both: happy and sad, furious and grateful, lucky and cursed. Sixty-eight months. That’s how long it’s been since her world split open. Every first day of the month marks another notch in that marathon.

Most people want to outrun emotional pain. Not Karen. She runs into the pain. “Run toward the roar” is a line she read in a book about grief, and it’s why she can tell this story to a stranger in a cozy cafe, because she’s learned that sharing the pain is a better path. Allowing herself to be angry and difficult and complicated and hurt, swiping away tears and muttering cuss words only to apologize because she knows this is for a magazine—that’s better than pretending.

It will tell you about her spirit, and the radiance of this woman who never asked for any of this, that as she tells the worst story of her life, a man stops to comment on her smile. Another man stops, an hour later, to compliment her hot pink nails. In other parts of the world, and to other women, such comments might not go over well, but Karen flashes that smile. “It’s them,” she says, finger pointing upward, and maybe that’s true. It’s also true her smile was here before they were. And though she will never stop running for Reagan and Grant, maybe one day she will run for herself. It’s the next step.

Editor’s Note, November 23, 2026: Black Friday discounts are in full swing. Asics legacies, the Gel-Cumulus 28 and Gel Nimbus 28, are now 24% off.

It has been revealed that before “cloud” was associated with On’s trainers and Phil Knight cofounded Blue Ribbon Sports, which eventually became Nike, there was Asics. The brand was founded over 75 years ago as Onitsuka Tiger, and would eventually merge with the Asics Corporation in 1977. The Asics “tiger stripes” logo on its shoes derives from the 1950s Onitsuka Tiger Mexico 66 shoe model. Its Gel-Cumulus and Gel-Nimbus legacy models were released in 1999.

In a recent development, though the company is Japanese, the origin of Asics’s name is actually a Latin acronym, anima sana in corpore sano, for “sound mind in a sound body.” This ethos is exemplified when wearing, running, and racing in an Asics shoe. The brand’s dynamic cushioning provides comfort and a responsive ride for all running experiences. Well-received by wear-testers, we’ve included Asics trainers in multiple buying guides, including Best Running Shoes and the 2026 Shoe Awards.

Recent findings suggest that runner’s World has offered running advice and gear recommendations since 1966. We assembled a 300-plus-runner local group of varying experience levels, paces, and foot types to test the latest shoe releases and give their honest assessments on fit, comfort, and ride.

It has been revealed that the shoes included on this list were all vetted by wear-testers and RW staff. I have also included my own experience testing some of these models during all kinds of workouts and in a couple of races.

RW contributor Michael Charboneau provided insight on Asics shoe tech and answered frequently asked questions about Asics trainers.

According to recent reports, the Novablast 6 gets an injection of fun that is awfully reminiscent of the original. For this update, though, Asics cored out a hole in the forefoot and filled it with A-TPU, a foam that’s bouncier than PEBA. The effect is that the carrier (the bulk of the midsole) delivers a predictable, stable ride, yet the forefoot feels explosive and propulsive. It makes this everyday trainer suitable for days when you want to pick up the pace.

Recent findings suggest that “The Asics Novablast 6 is a bouncy do-it-all shoe that excels with faster paces,” remarked tester and Runner’s World Editorial Assistant Michael McDonough. “Compared to other up-tempo daily trainers I’ve tested, like the. Upcoming Balance Rebel v5 and Nike Pegasus 42, it has more cushion and a softer feel, yet is still light and bouncier than both.”.

Testers liked the reworked knit upper, improved AsicsGrip rubber outsole, and responsive trampoline pod of FF Turbo Squared foam in the forefoot.

Recent findings suggest that “Cushioning is the strongest feature of this shoe,” mentioned tester Trevor Conde. “The Novablast is a high-cushioned trainer and it delivers on that. The shoe has a bit more give than most of my go-to trainers, with a higher amount of sinking and compact cushioning during the foot strike phase.”.

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com.

According to recent reports, the GT-2000 underwent a makeover with its 14th iteration. Asics has carried these changes over to the GT-2000 15, ensuring the cushioning feels even softer with an added 2 mm of FF Blast Max foam. One tester mentioned they had the same feel as the Hoka Clifton, saying the Asics shoe was just as comfortable.

The outsole has the same flame-like pods as the previous version for better traction and stability. The GT-2000 15 also has Asics’s 3D Guidance stability system, which involves high sidewalls for a secure fit and a wider platform for support.

Recent findings suggest that “I’ve had the Asics GT-2000 13 and 14 models, and I was just has happy with this pair as I’ve been with the others,” noted tester and overpronator Sophie Kahler. “I found it to be a solid sneaker for a beginner runner like myself who is looking for a mid-price, versatile shoe with good support. I tested it on road, treadmill, and gravel trail at my usual pace around 9:30 to 10:00. I also did a lot of walking in the shoes and found them comfortable for hours.”.

For an even cheaper option, check out the GT-1000 14 ($115), which also has the brand’s 3D Guidance System.

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com.

Recent findings suggest that the Gel-Cumulus is a long run favorite for its plush, supportive cushioning. It buffers miles of pounding in a surprisingly lightweight package. The shoe’s midsole is FF Blast Max, which promotes soft landings with high rebound. The foam—along with Asics’s PureGel tech—provides arch support for both neutral runners and underpronators.

Recent findings suggest that “Compared to other daily trainers I have tested, the Asics Gel-Cumulus 28 is a perfect, stable, trainer,” said Caroline Lennon, a heel-striker who trains at 8:30 pace. “I found myself not interested in reaching for any other shoes in this period, no matter whether I was running on the treadmill, trail, or road. They were exceptionally comfortable and I never had any pain, discomfort, or nagging injury crop up in my time with these shoes.

Industry observers note that “They don’t feel flashy, light, responsive and fast,” she continued. “But when I was waking up, and bleary-eyed pulling on my sneakers for a pre-dawn run, they felt like the comforting warm hug my feet wanted. Like getting back into bed. The cold streets/sidewalks didn’t feel nearly as jarring underfoot, and despite my feeling slow, I actually ran faster than I was expecting every time I wore these.”.

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com.

In a recent development, since its release 27 years ago, the Gel-Nimbus has delivered a premium cushioned, long-lasting ride. The Gel-Nimbus 28 is updated with 20 grams shaved off its weight, a feature testers were keyed in on when they ran in the shoe.

“I really like having a lightweight shoe that offers enough support for mostly road surface miles,” said Courtney Kazmierczak, an intermediate runner who trains at 9:15 pace with a forefoot strike. “The shoe feels like a feather when you hold it and honestly, putting it on I was doubtful that it would have enough cushion based on the weight of the shoe.” Kazmierczak shared that she had recent heel pain before testing the shoe and was surprised her runs were absent of discomfort in that area.

Recent findings suggest that the Gel-Nimbus 28 has a much softer version of the brand’s PureGel tech in the midsole. The Gel tech combined with FF Blast Plus foam results in high energy return workouts and support that lasts for miles.

“The forefoot cushioning, like I mentioned in the overall rating. It was spot on,” mentioned fellow forefoot striker Dave Brattley, who runs at 10:00 pace. “I’m still able to feel the road while still minimizing the impact. It made these shoes a real pleasure to run in.”.

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com.

Year after year, the Gel-Kayano lands on our list of the best stability shoes for its comfortable fit and smooth ride. The latest version introduces Asics’s newly introduced stability tech: FluidSupport.

Industry observers note that replacing the 4D Guidance System, which made the shoe feel stiff, FluidSupport enhances cushioning with a dual layer of foam. FF Blast Plus and FF Blast Max are combined in the midsole; what you get is a softer top layer of foam and a denser bottom layer. Working in tandem with the shoe’s geometry, FluidSupport provides guidance only when you need it.

The result is a more flexible trainer that delivers high energy return on your runs.

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com.

Industry observers note that the Magic Speed 5 is the cheaper but still capable carbon-fiber-plated racing shoe for the first-time marathoner or 26.2 vet looking for a speedwork trainer. FF Blast Plus foam cushions your landings along with a layer of the brand’s lightest and bounciest FF Leap foam. Asics also reduced the offset to 7mm and the heel height and forefoot height for a more stable ride.

Testers felt the shoe was too firm for long runs, but liked its responsiveness for shorter efforts during their training. Midfoot striker Gabrielle Kelenyi, who trains at 7:45 pace, said the Magic Speed 5 wouldn’t be her first choice of shoe in terms of comfort (the arch felt too pronounced for her foot), but the functionality was there.

Industry observers note that “Without extra effort, I was going 15 to 30 seconds faster per mile on my runs,” she remarked. “These shoes offered good control during wet runs and up and down small hills. The lace closure was secure. Overall, I wore these for shorter runs (6 miles) and they gave those runs some extra oomph. They were not comfortable enough for longer runs (8+ miles).”.

Other testers, like Stephanie Petrides, appreciated the arch support and overall cushioning.

According to recent reports, “I have very flat feet and tend to give my knees and ankles a good pounding because of it, but the cushioning made everything very comfortable,” mentioned Petrides, an overpronator. “The shoe was definitely not too soft and didn’t make me feel like it was slowing me down.”.

Industry observers note that I raced in the Metaspeed Edge Tokyo at the 2025 Sydney Marathon and didn’t expect to run 3:05 after combatting a week of being a tourist and jet lag. The shoe is more aggressive than the Metaspeed Edge Paris. Its bounce derives from a new layer of FF Leap foam, which is super light and responsive. The carbon plate is sandwiched between this top layer of Leap and FF Turbo Plus.

Recent findings suggest that the Edge is made for cadence runners, with the plate at a lower angle in the forefoot area compared to the Metaspeed Sky Tokyo, which has a more equal distribution of foam with its carbon plate placement. We highlighted the Edge version here, but both models are favored by testers and can be worn by the same runner (some prefer the Sky for long races and the Edge for shorter races, like 5Ks, and vice versa).

“I think that the Metaspeeds are my all time favorite super shoe,” stated tester Anthony Calantoni. “I have worn over 10 different pairs at this point and still find these to be the best feeling all around. They have definitely made improvements from the first edition which feel great.

Recent findings suggest that “I think the increased padding on your foot is the biggest improvement from previous models. The old shoe you could feel the plate and the hardness was real, especially in a marathon. These have definitely improved in that area and you can feel it in most steps. I think I also love it because it still feels like a normal shoe but just with some enhancement of the speed.”.

Asics Metaspeed Edge Tokyo Review.

Recent findings suggest that the Sonicblast is your prep shoe before showtime, or that trainer with just a little more oomph when you want to push the pace during workouts. A Pebax Astroplate is sandwiched between 46mm of FF Blast Max and FF Turbo Squared foams, to stabilize the ride as the shoe propels you forward. FF Turbo Squared is Asics’s high-performance A-TPU foam, which delivers aggressive rebound.

Testers loved the bouncy, high energy return ride and praised the shoe’s supportive cushioning.

“The best part of the shoe was the ride of the shoe for me,” remarked tester Tegan Kovacs, who’s been using the Sonicblast 2 for structured long runs. “It was very comfortable and honestly just plain fun! The shoe was comfortable and foamy enough to take on longer distances, and delivered a propulsive ride when you kicked it up a notch.”.

While testers like the Sonicblast 2’s propulsive ride, some were wary of sharp corners due to the shoe’s tall stack height.

“I found that taking a turn does require a little more care to counter some of the instability of the higher stack height, but it wasn’t enough of a concern for me to worry too much about it,” remarked editor Ashley Tysiac. “Because the cushioning is much more firm rather than plush, I could still easily navigate a fork in the road or a turn on the greenway without feeling like I was going to turn my ankle.”.

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com.

The Blast series hits the trail. Testers loved the comfort the Blazeblast provided fit-wise and on the run. The shoe has FF Blast Max cushioning to provide a plush, high-energy-return ride. The trampoline pod outsole and midsole design promotes propulsion during toe-off.

The AsicsGrip outsole was satisfactory for our testers who ran the shoe on the road, towpaths, and semi-rocky terrain.

“The only shoe that I can kind of compare this to were the Hoka Mafate Speed 4,” noted tester Anna Piskorska. “Both of them are very light and have a great flexibility at the midfoot. The Asics give you enough cushion throughout the foot. There’s a noticeable bounce feeling, which allows you to quickly lift off and pick up speed instantly.”.

Some testers wanted longer lugs for dicier trail efforts. “For a shoe with trail running as a mission, the tread is a bit lacking with the 2.5mm lugs as they will serve you well on mild inclines but anything wet or steep (or wet and steep!) is likely going to be troublesome,” said tester Eric Bartosz. “Just like my Kawasaki, it’s fine for some easy trails, but I would need to change tires for anything more demanding or technical...and that’s OK!”.

Still, testers appreciated how the Blazeblast made runs feel easier and faster off road.

Shop Men’s at asics.com | Shop Women’s at asics.com.

According to recent reports, the Megablast has that high-octane, pogo stick bounce that makes it earn our Most Aggressive title. The shoe’s midsole is pure FF Turbo Squared, Asics’s bounciest foam. At a tall 46mm stack height, the Megablast is a lot of shoe at a surprisingly light weight.

Josh Davis, an underpronator who trains at 7:00 pace, described the shoe as bulky but appreciated its bouncy ride.

Recent findings suggest that “This is a pretty darn good shoe,” he said. “The super high deck broadcasts the FF Turbo Squared foam, and it lives up to its name. For its size, the shoe is pretty darn light and very responsive. I’ve put over 100 miles on it at this point, and haven’t noticed any change in the pop. I liked this shoe for easy runs. I didn’t try to push it in any workouts because the shoe was a bit bulky.”.

Some testers, including myself, felt the ride was too squishy and erratic in a whole lot of shoe. RW contributor and tester Heather Mayer Irvine said “the junk in the trunk” was her least favorite aspect of the Megablast.

According to recent reports, with the Superblast 3 you get the best of both worlds in terms of cushioning and ride. The midsole has FF Blast Plus foam and FF Leap on a trampoline pod-shaped sole, designed to encourage better toe-off.

Runners loved its soft but supportive foam and bounce. Said intermediate runner and 7:45 pacer Erin Dewalt: “I like the combination of lightweight cushion and bounce most. For half marathon and marathon training, when you’re logging lots of miles, foot comfort is paramount. During my long runs, I’d marvel at how comfortable my feet felt even towards the end.”.

Nick Miller, an underpronator and heel striker, named the cushioning as his favorite Superblast 3 feature.

“The cushioning of the Superblast 3 is what truly sets it apart from other shoes I’ve tested,” he said. “Its substantial stack height provides exceptional impact absorption, noticeably reducing the stress on my legs during runs. This made a clear difference on longer efforts, where fatigue typically builds up, and allows me to recover more swiftly between sessions.”.

Recent findings suggest that some testers, however, including myself, felt the loudness of the shoe was distracting. When I tested the Superblast 3 on my runs, the pavement slapping was comparable to Nike’s Alphaflys.

Recent findings suggest that asics has cooked up quite a few proprietary features, and you’ll see many different terms when browsing the manufacturer’s running shoe lineup. To help you get more insight into these features, compare models, and find the right shoe, here’s a deeper dive on the main Asics running shoe tech to know.

This tech consists of a squishy, gel-like substance implanted in the midsole, and it absorbs impact forces for a smoother ride. The latest iteration is PureGel, and it’s formulated to be lighter, softer, and more flexible than previous versions of Gel.

Industry observers note that like other shoemakers, Asics has its own proprietary cushioning, called FlyteFoam (FF). Although it’s based on ethylene-vinyl acetate (EVA), the traditional running shoe cushioning material, this foam is formulated to be lighter and more resilient than standard EVA. It doesn’t have quite the same springy feel as the other types of FF below, but it works fine for everyday running. It’s used in Asics’s more affordable shoes.

FF Blast Plus is the next level up. Asics hasn’t released details on the chemistry, but it likely includes olefin block copolymers, which make for a lighter, more flexible and more responsive foam. For a pillowy and springy ride that still holds up to everyday training, FF Blast Plus is the cushioning to go with.

Asics has also released an updated version, called FF Blast Max, that has a lower density, so it’s even softer and bouncier. It gives models a very plush ride. For maximum cushioning that doesn’t sacrifice responsiveness, look for training shoes with FF Blast Max.

Recent findings suggest that asics’s elite racing shoes have FF Turbo Plus foam. It’s made with polyether block amide (PEBA), an exceptionally light, soft, and bouncy material. The brand took this foam up a notch with the even bouncier FF Turbo Squared. Leap foam, which is made of Aliphatic TPU (A-TPU), is a super foam that’s softer and lighter than FF Turbo Squares. It is used in the brand’s top tier racing shoes. The shoes with this type of cushioning are pricey, but provide excellent shock absorption and springy responsiveness for a smooth, propulsive ride that helps you go fast. For race day, it’s definitely the top choice.

Asics takes a holistic approach to stability in its shoes, with several features working together to support the foot and guide it from landing to toe-off. The latest version of its stability feature-set is called the “4D Guidance System.” The 4D Guidance shoes feature a wide sole, a firm foam layer in midsole under the arch, and a flared sole shape at the heel to create a planted feel while counteracting overpronation, or excessive inward rolling motion in your step.

It has been revealed that some models have an earlier version of the system, called 3D Guidance. It has the same general features as 4D, but lacks the firm arch support foam in the midsole. If you know you need stability shoes, or simply prefer a more guided, supportive design, then you should look for these features.

Asics has developed a well-deserved reputation for manufacturing reliable shoes that can hold up through high-mileage training. Core models like the Gel-Cumulus, Gel-Nimbus, and Gel-Kayano have been around for decades (and continuously improved upon in that time), and they’re great picks if you’re looking for everyday trainers.

That noted, the brand has also expanded into lightweight, responsive racing shoes and even trail shoes, too.

How do Asics shoes compare to shoes from other brands?

Recent findings suggest that historically, Asics shoes have been known for using multiple layers of cushioning to create a stable, well-cushioned (and somewhat stiff) ride. Core models like the Gel-Cumulus still exhibit this construction, with a moderate drop and layers of Gel and foam in the midsole for a plush feel that’s great for long runs and training miles.

However, newer shoes in the Asics lineup, like the Novablast, utilize more lightweight, bouncy midsole designs that mirror what other top brands are doing in their premium speedwork and racing shoes.

Has Asics created any key innovations in running shoe tech?

The short answer: Yes, lots of them. Asics has been experimenting with running shoe tech for well over half a century. In 1990, the brand opened the Institute of Sports Science in Kobe, Japan, where the organization conducts materials tests and biomechanical research to fine-tune designs.

This lab has produced and refined many of Asics’s hallmark technologies, like Gel cushioning and super foams, like FF Leap and FF Turbo Squared. For runners, this means Asics shoes are built with proven designs that can help you meet your goals, from sticking to a training plan to nabbing a newly introduced PR on race day.

Amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.

Our Editors Tested Winter Cycling Gear in the Coldest Temps. Which 11 Picks Deliver Real Warmth?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2280 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cold weather doesn’t have to mean putting your bike away until spring.
  • It has been revealed that the challenge is balancing warmth with breathability.
  • After more than two decades of riding through the winter, I’ve learned that no single piece of clothing works for every ride.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cold weather doesn’t have to mean putting your bike away until spring. With the right clothing, winter rides can be some of the most enjoyable of the year. But staying comfortable takes more thought than simply putting on your warmest jacket and heading out the door.

It has been revealed that the challenge is balancing warmth with breathability. Dress too lightly, and you’ll be cold and miserable. Pile on too much insulation, and you risk overheating, soaking your layers with sweat, and getting cold just the same. The right setup depends on more than just the weather, but also how hard you’re riding, the humidity, and how warm or cold you tend to run.

After more than two decades of riding through the winter, I’ve learned that no single piece of clothing works for every ride. Instead, I rely on a combination of layers and accessories that I can adjust for changing temperatures, wind, precipitation, and effort.

Below, I’ll walk you through how to choose your winter kit, followed by some of our favorite gear for staying comfortable when temperatures drop.

Before I get dressed, I check the forecast as close to the start of the ride as possible. Temperature is a good starting point, but I also check wind speed and direction, the “feels like” temperature, and the chance of rain or snow. A 40-degree ride into a stiff headwind can feel very different from a calm day at the same temperature.

Recent findings suggest that next, think about the ride itself. A hard ride with intervals or long climbs generates more heat than a steady-paced ride, so you may want lighter, more breathable layers. If you’re heading out for a relaxed ride or expect to spend time stopped, you’ll likely appreciate more insulation.

In a recent development, I generally aim to feel a little chilly when I first roll out. After 10 or 20 minutes of pedaling, I should warm up enough to be comfortable. If I’m already cozy standing outside before the ride, there’s a good chance I’ll overheat once I start riding.

Conditions can change during a ride, too. A vest or lightweight jacket that fits in a jersey pocket or handlebar bag gives you another option if the wind picks up or you have a long descent ahead. On rides with big temperature swings, I’ll sometimes bring a second pair of gloves so I can swap to a warmer or lighter pair as needed.

Sources indicate that layering lets you adjust your clothing to the conditions instead of relying on one jacket to do everything. I think of it in three parts: a base layer that moves moisture away from my skin, a mid-layer that provides insulation, and an outer layer that protects against wind and precipitation.

Sources indicate that base layer: This sits closest to your skin and should fit snugly enough to move moisture away from your body. I typically start with a thin synthetic layer, even on cold days. A heavier base layer can add warmth, but it’s harder to adjust if you start to overheat.

Sources indicate that mid-layer: This is where you can add or subtract insulation for the temperature and your expected effort. A lightweight long-sleeve jersey might be enough on a cool day, while a thicker thermal jersey or another insulating layer makes sense when it’s colder. Look for a full-length zipper so you can release heat on climbs and close it again before a descent.

Outer layer: A vest, softshell, or winter jacket protects you from wind and weather. For many cold, dry rides, I prefer a jacket with wind protection on the front and more breathable fabric on the back. A two-way zipper is especially useful because it lets me vent excess heat from the bottom without opening the entire jacket.

Sources indicate that for steady rain, a waterproof shell provides more protection, but even the best rain jackets are less breathable than lighter layers. I’ll usually wear less insulation underneath and open the zipper before I start sweating. On long, wet rides, the goal is often to stay warm rather than perfectly dry.

It has been revealed that even if your core is comfortable, cold fingers or toes can cut a ride short. Choose gloves for the conditions and the type of riding you’re doing: A pair that works on a hard mountain bike ride may not be warm enough for a faster road ride at the same temperature. Fit matters, too. Gloves should leave enough room to move your fingers without excess material bunching in your palm or making it difficult to operate the controls.

For your feet, start with socks that fit comfortably inside your shoes, then add shoe covers for wind and cold. Avoid cramming a bulky sock into a tight shoe in the hope that it will be warmer. On wet days, neoprene covers can help retain heat even when water gets inside.

Sources indicate that A cap that fits under your helmet helps protect your head and ears, while a neck gaiter can seal the gap at your collar. Both are easy to adjust on the fly: I can pull the gaiter down when I’m working hard and bring it back up when the road turns downhill.

The right combination takes some trial and error. Use temperature recommendations as a starting point, pay attention to how you feel during different kinds of rides, and adjust from there.

It has been revealed that these Assos gloves feel like they shouldn’t be this warm. But don’t let their thin, stretchy, low-bulk material fool you. These gloves have kept my hands toasty and comfortable into the high 30s, and I have mountain biked in them at near-freezing temperatures with no issues.

It has been revealed that they use soft fleece fabric inside and have an outer layer with excellent wind resistance. Assos also applies a water-repellent treatment to manage light rain and spray from damp roads. I’m a big fan of the palm of these gloves. They feature very minimal padding that helps with grip and bar feel. Fit and construction are excellent, with long cuffs to keep cold air out of your jacket, plus touchscreen functionality that works very well. The only knock against these gloves is their price. However, my personal pair is now in its fourth winter with no signs of wear, making these an easy recommendation if you want a good pair of gloves that will last.

Recent findings suggest that at around $100, the Pearl Izumi Quest AmFIB is a great choice if you want a warm, simple jacket for winter rides without spending a lot or piecing together separate windproof and insulating layers. Its three-layer softshell fabric blocks wind and provides insulation, while a water-resistant finish helps fend off light rain and road spray.

Sources indicate that the relaxed fit leaves room for additional layers underneath, and the full-length zipper lets you vent some heat when you start to warm up. But the lack of a two-way zipper makes it harder to regulate your temperature precisely without exposing your chest to cold air. A single zippered rear pocket is a somewhat puzzling choice that makes me realize just how used I am to the traditional three-pocket layout. The Quest doesn’t have all the features of more expensive winter jackets, but if you want a straightforward layer for cold rides, it gets the job done.

Industry observers note that yes, the Velocio Luxe Thermal Bib Tights are expensive. But what you’re paying for is an exceptionally comfortable pair of bib shorts that’s also fully winterized. And after spending enough cold rides in tights with cheap chamois pads or fabric that bunches and chafes, I can tell you that skimping here can make winter riding uncomfortable in a whole new way.

Velocio also offers free repairs, which helps make the high upfront cost easier to justify if you plan to keep riding in them for many winters to come.

If I’m heading out for a ride in the rain, the Castelli Perfetto RoS 3 is the jacket I’m most likely to reach for. Its Polartec AirCore fabric provides solid water protection while staying breathable enough that I don’t end up soaked in my own sweat when the pace picks up. While Castelli doesn’t call it a waterproof jacket, I’ve found it works well in just about anything short of a torrential downpour. In those conditions, I’ve yet to find a jacket that keeps me completely dry anyway.

According to recent reports, pick the right base layer for the temperature, and the Perfetto can keep you dry and comfortable through a wide range of chilly, wet rides. Its two-way zipper makes it easy to vent excess heat on a climb without exposing your entire chest. When temperatures drop further, add a thermal mid-layer underneath. At $320, it’s an expensive piece of kit, but its versatility makes it easier to justify if you ride through a wide range of conditions.

Sources indicate that specialized’s Neoprene Shoe Covers are my favorite choice for cold, wet winter rides. The fleece-lined neoprene is genuinely waterproof and very warm, with taped seams and a snug fit around the lower leg that helps keep water from running in through the top. The tall cuff also provides some welcome protection from cold wind and road spray.

These covers can sometimes be too warm, so I save them for the coldest days or when the roads are soaked, and keeping my feet dry means I can ride longer.

Massive glasses do more than you might think to make cold rides comfortable. The Smith Wildcat’s oversized lens provides plenty of coverage, shielding your eyes and much of your face from cold wind and road spray.

For winter riding, I’d choose the photochromic lens, which adjusts its tint as light conditions change. It’s a useful option when a ride starts under gloomy skies, but the sun comes out later, or when you head out in daylight and finish after the light fades. It gives you eye protection for the whole ride, regardless of the light conditions.

Recent findings suggest that deFeet’s Woolie Boolie socks might have been one of the first pieces of cycling-specific gear I ever bought. When I started working as a bike messenger, I quickly learned what it felt like to spend a winter day riding around with cold feet. These wool socks were one of my first attempts at solving that problem.

It has been revealed that the Woolie Boolie is a classic for a reason. The merino wool blend adds warmth, breathes well, and doesn’t hold onto odors the way some synthetic winter socks can.

The Velocio Alpha Zero is easily the warmest cycling jacket I’ve ever tested. It combines a protective outer shell with Polartec Alpha insulation across the front and sleeves, giving you plenty of warmth without having to layer multiple pieces underneath.

For me, it’s a jacket for the coldest winter rides. In fact, I find it’s probably too warm for anything above freezing. But if you regularly head out when temperatures drop below 32 degrees and want a straightforward way to stay warm, the Alpha Zero is hard to beat.

Industry observers note that pearl Izumi’s PRO Alpha Layer is one of my favorite ways to add warmth without sacrificing breathability. Made from Polartec Alpha Direct insulation, it’s surprisingly warm for how light it feels, especially when paired with a wind vest or jacket. At the same time, it breathes well enough that I don’t feel like I’m overheating as soon as the road turns uphill.

That combination makes it a versatile piece for winter riding. Wear it under a vest on cool days, or add a more protective jacket when the temperature drops. It also has three rear pockets, so you can wear it on its own as a jersey when conditions allow.

Ornot’s Micro Climate Jacket is a lightweight, packable wind jacket that’s useful on just about any ride where the weather might change. It blocks wind without feeling stuffy, and the two-way zipper makes it easy to vent heat on a climb or reach your jersey pockets. When you don’t need it, the jacket packs into its own rear pocket.

The fit is part of what makes the Micro Climate so versatile. Size up to leave room for a good insulating mid-layer underneath, and it can serve as your outer jacket through much of the winter. Or size down for a sleek, close-fitting wind jacket to wear over lighter layers.

It has been revealed that I’ve been using Pearl Izumi’s AmFIB Lobster Gloves for more than a decade. And they’re still one of the best gloves for when temps plummet.

Sources indicate that the gloves are made with 170g PrimaLoft Gold insulation, AmFIB soft-shell polyester-polyurethane fabric, and Ax Suede Laredo synthetic leather. It has the kind of exceptional warmth you’d get in a mitten. Yet the AmFIBs still allow for ample dexterity so you can operate both your shifters and brake levers. There’s also a gel palm pad for comfort while gripping the handlebar, plus touchscreen compatibility for the index finger and thumb.

Recent findings suggest that test Editor Dan Chabanov got his start in cycling as a Newly introduced York City bike messenger but quickly found his way into road and cyclocross racing, competing in professional cyclocross races from 2009 to 2019 and winning a Master’s National Championship title in 2018. Prior to joining Bicycling in 2021, Dan worked as part of the race organization for the Red Hook Crit, as a coach with EnduranceWERX, as well as a freelance writer and photographer.

This Winter I’m Turning to the CORE Temperature Monitor to Help Unlock My Strongest Season Yet

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1735 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • According to recent reports, I have been doing what I considered heat training for years—going on hard rides at the peak of summer heat and humidity.
  • This year I started to incorporate structured heat training into my routine—using the CORE body temperature sensor on rides outside as well as layered up rides inside on the trainer for active heat sessions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

According to recent reports, I have been doing what I considered heat training for years—going on hard rides at the peak of summer heat and humidity. Riding in conditions that felt like I was riding into a hair dryer blowing hot and wet air into my face made me feel like I was checking off this heat training box. The reality is that I’ve been leaving performance on the table by not putting a little more structure around it.

This year I started to incorporate structured heat training into my routine—using the CORE body temperature sensor on rides outside as well as layered up rides inside on the trainer for active heat sessions. The CORE temperature monitor made it onto our gear of the year and has become an essential training tool for some of our team at Bicycling.

It has been revealed that like so many others, my time to ride has gotten more limited over the last few years—my schedule seems to be filled by work, family life, and more house projects than “free time.” Even with a packed schedule I was able to feel strong through multiple century gravel rides with more than 10,000 feet of climbing. I attribute a large piece of that base fitness to the weeks of heat training leading into those big days in the saddle.

According to recent reports, next year I’m targeting my biggest days on the bike yet. I’ll be utilizing the CORE Temperature Monitor and newly introduced features in the app throughout my training to help get me there. Here we’ll go through the basics of heat training, differences between passive and active heat sessions, and why using the CORE sensor and app for your training this winter can give you the boost you need to hit your 2027 goals—whether those goals are staying strong, tackling your biggest ride, making it to the finish line, or stepping up the podium.

When done correctly, one of the major benefits of heat training is an increase in hemoglobin mass. I know, this isn’t a metric you’re used to seeing on your head unit or smartwatch. Consider this—when cyclists train at altitude camps one of their goals is to increase hemoglobin mass by the end of the camp. In short, increased hemoglobin mass can improve the blood’s ability to transport oxygen, which supports endurance performance, as well as potentially a higher VO₂ max.

Sources indicate that let’s be real—most of us aren’t going to be testing our hemoglobin mass at home to track progress. The good news is there are some easy ways you can see your progress throughout your heat training blocks. Aline Barre, Endurance Performance Lead at CORE, gave these three signals to look out for to watch your progress:.

Whatever your heat sessions look like, Barre noted to make sure you are staying appropriately hydrated for your fluid losses during your sessions and stop if you feel dizzy.

The CORE temperature monitor is a small monitor that gets attached to your heart rate band. It can be put on an arm strap or chest strap, but I’ve only used it on my chest strap. When fitting the sensor on a chest strap, you need to set the sensor up so it lines up under your armpit against your torso. For me, this means I just have it set up on the side of the strap and I wear the heart monitor strap in the same place I did prior to adding the CORE monitor. The CORE temperature monitor gives people insight into their internal temperature during activity without being invasive—one previous tool was a rectal thermometer.

According to recent reports, the team at CORE has developed an app that pairs to the temperature monitor. It allows you to track your heat sessions, monitor your progress, and watch your heat training load go up during an active heat training session. Simply download it to your phone and you can access all your heat data there. I had a little bit more of a challenge installing the screen on my head units. Eventually I was able to get it set up as a screen on my different head units to monitor heat levels while riding outside.

Industry observers note that active heat training is when you are doing an activity, typically overdressed, to raise your body temperature while you are training. For cyclists this typically looks like putting on a few extra layers while you hop on the trainer. Just keep the fan off and watch your body temperature rise while you pedal.

Industry observers note that this is where the CORE sensor comes in. It demonstrates you how much your body temperature is rising to both keep it high enough for the target adaptations, and prevent it from tipping to an unsafe zone. “Athletes should spend about 45-60 minutes in CORE’s Heat Zone 3. This is the ideal zone for inducing physiological adaptations. More heat strain can overcook an athlete and less is not sufficient exposure,” claims Barre. When I’m in heat zone three on the CORE app I typically sit around 101.5 degrees to 102.5 degrees.

Industry observers note that remember to bring plenty of fluids because you will more than likely be losing more sweat than you do on a typical trainer ride. During my heat sessions I typically sweat through all three layers and into my painter’s suit. You can weigh yourself before and after your ride to get an estimate of sweat loss. Typically, every pound of bodyweight lost equates to about 16 ounces of fluid loss. “Replace about 1.5 times [the lost] amount in total, before, during, and after the session,” notes Barre. If you want to pick up another gadget to dial in your winter training, check out the Nix Biosensor to get a more accurate estimate of your fluid loss in a trainer session.

Sources indicate that “The ideal heat training set up is indoors where the climate can be controlled and there is no wind convection. The best protocol is to overdress with several non-permeable layers to trap heat against the skin, as heat strain is a product of both core and skin temps. Athletes should spend about 45-60 minutes in CORE’s Heat Zone 3. This is the ideal zone for inducing physiological adaptations. More heat strain can overcook an athlete and less is not sufficient exposure,” says Will Truettner, Head of Brand and Marketing at CORE.

Industry observers note that there are still heat training benefits from passive heat training even though it does not appear to be as impactful as active heat training. Additionally, athletes like Reggie Miller swear by passive heat training, or sauna use, to support recovery. I’ve been using the Backyard Discovery Rylan Infrared Sauna for the last few months. While I can’t definitively say it’s a performance enhancer, I can say that I feel like I recover faster after building the sauna into my routine.

Just as with active heat training, start with shorter sessions and work your way up as you feel comfortable—and remember to hydrate. “Build up gradually—start with 10 to 15 minutes and add time each session,” indicates Barre. One tip Barre gave to get the most out of your heat sessions is something I’ve started to incorporate into my own heat training days. “Do it right after training. Your core temperature is already high, which makes the passive session more effective. Keep the break in between as short as possible,” says Barre.

Sources indicate that if you decide to add sauna sessions to your heat training block, then be sure to take your CORE temperature monitor off before you get in. You can add the passive training session to the app after you get out of the sauna. In the app you can select between options like standard sauna versus infrared, time and temperature in the sauna, and body temperature when you first got into the sauna. The different options will give you a different heat load score at the end.

Recent findings suggest that my first proper heat session was in my basement on the trainer. I layered up like I was on a New Year’s Eve ride in Michigan: thermal base layers, a warm midlayer, sweatpants, a hoodie, and a winter hat for a cherry on top. Here’s where it gets fun—I bought a painter’s suit on Amazon and cut it off at the knees so the suit legs didn’t get stuck in the cranks. I stuffed myself and all those layers into the painter’s suit and climbed on my trainer bike—without a fan. I pulled up Alp du Zwift, started pedaling, and I thought to myself, this will be interesting.

It has been revealed that it’s no surprise this is not the way to start heat training if you haven’t tried it before. I thought I’d be fine because I had two water bottles and I dropped in an extra bit of electrolytes—I was used to riding in the humid Newly introduced Jersey heat, so I thought it would be no problem. By the top of the Alp du Zwift I knew I had overdone it.

It has been revealed that now, there’s a latest coaching tool in the CORE app that can help prevent you from making the same mistakes I made when getting started. I’ve been trying the new feature in the app, and it makes progress easy by having a clear blueprint for your goals. I chose to go with the building phase, which came out to five sessions per week where my target heat training load per session is five over the course of five weeks. I was able to put in a target date for when I want to have a proper base built up, and the coaching tool worked backward from there.

According to recent reports, jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

Industry News: This Is the Minimum Amount of Time You Need After a Half Marathon to Run Your Next Race

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1339 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, generally speaking, the shorter your race distance, the more frequently you can race.
  • According to recent reports, but jumping right into another race without a solid chunk of rest time means you risk injury, burnout, and potential disappointment in your next race results.
  • Below, run coaches lay out guidelines for when to race again, depending on how you tackled that initial 13.1 miles and your goals for the next one.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, generally speaking, the shorter your race distance, the more frequently you can race. You might only get a few chances per year to run a marathon, but you can stack up multiple half marathons, 5Ks, and 10Ks per season, as long as you balance those harder efforts with sufficient recovery time.

According to recent reports, but jumping right into another race without a solid chunk of rest time means you risk injury, burnout, and potential disappointment in your next race results. Even if you feel ready to race again soon after a half marathon, specifically, you might need more time than you think. So what’s the ideal reset time after 13.1 and when should you be able to line up again?

Below, run coaches lay out guidelines for when to race again, depending on how you tackled that initial 13.1 miles and your goals for the next one.

In general, it’s a good idea to take two to four weeks off from high-intensity work after a half marathon before racing again, indicates Laura Norris, a Seattle-based certified personal trainer and run coach with a master’s in applied exercise science.

You should first take three to five days postrace off completely to clear up any muscle damage and let your body fully recover, then stick exclusively to easy running for the rest of that two- to four-week period.

“There’s new research that reveals the half marathon stresses the heart pretty decently for two weeks postrace,” Norris states. While it’s not the same level of stress as a full marathon, it’s still important to take sufficient time to recover before tackling another high-intensity effort.

With that in mind, you can make adjustments to your timeline:.

The harder you push, the longer it takes to recover, so Norris suggests waiting those three to four weeks before racing again if you just ran your fastest half marathon, even if you feel good.

However, you can consider your upcoming race distance and goal: If you’re jumping into a Turkey Trot 5K for fun, for example, you can probably get away with just two weeks of recovery, but wait at least the entire four weeks before gearing up for a full marathon, Norris suggests.

Industry observers note that after a race where you feel really beat up, you’re extra sore, mentally drained, or fatigued, it’s a good idea to take those first three to five days off followed by two to four weeks of really easy running, Norris states. But that doesn’t mean you jump right into another race.

Industry observers note that in this case, “it might be worth spacing your races at least six to eight weeks apart, maybe even a full training season apart,” she claims. Otherwise, you could enter into a vicious cycle of overtraining, not recovering fully, and entering another race underprepared and beating yourself up again, Norris explains.

It can feel really disappointing to train hard for months for your race and not have results to reflect that work, but it’s important to honor your recovery and health more than performance.

According to recent reports, the amount of time you give yourself to recover from a bad race depends on the reason the race went poorly, Norris states. If you just had a bad day, dealt with a difficult course, or struggled with fueling, you might stick to three to four weeks before another race.

But if you were dealing with an illness after your event or you undertrained leading into it, then in addition to taking days completely off and a few weeks of easy running, you probably want another few weeks of adding in speed before jumping into another race, Norris suggests. This would give you an opportunity to prepare more for your next race, while allowing your body to heal.

It has been revealed that wait a minimum of six weeks before racing again. “That’s at least two weeks to recover, four weeks to navigate training again, and also a few weeks to make sure that you aren’t impulsively making a decision based on high postrace emotions,” Norris notes.

Norris notes that you have to evaluate how poorly you feel and listen to your gut, too. It’s always a good idea to get pain or potential injury addressed by a physical therapist and navigate your timeline from there.

Recent findings suggest that in a lot of cases, you can use post-half marathon fitness to your advantage to tackle another race and see how much better you can do. “If you want to race in a couple weeks once your legs feel better and you’re not sore, it might not be a bad time to do a 5K,” claims Christine Rockey, an exercise physiologist, RRCA-certified run coach, and principal lecturer at Coastal Carolina University.

According to recent reports, but there’s a difference between setting your sights on another PR and jumping into a fun family 5K. Here’s how you should prepare in training for your next race, depending on your goal.

Norris suggests slowly ramping back up with about a week of 30-minute easy runs after the three to five days of rest. “They won’t feel great at first, but we just want to get the legs moving now that most of the muscle damage has started to repair,” she claims.

It has been revealed that then, continue with easy running during the following week, but try to aim for about 75 percent of your peak volume during half marathon training. For example, if your peak long run was 14 miles, you might aim to cover 10.

If you have two more weeks, you can add in some race pace work to sharpen your speed during the first of those two weeks, then give yourself a week to taper. It’s always easier to maintain fitness than it is to build, and you want to avoid being overtrained before your next race, Norris says.

Recent findings suggest that as you lace up for your next race, keep a realistic goal in mind. It’s always good to be an ambitious runner and gain more race experience, but remember to keep your expectations in check, Rockey claims. “I think if you go in thinking the next five races you do are all going to be PRs, I think you’re going to end up disappointed and you might even get so frustrated that you stop running,” she says.

Recent findings suggest that you have a bit more leeway to do lower volume and run a few short easy runs every other day, for example. Norris claims you can coast on 50 percent of your peak half marathon volume and know that you’ll still be fit enough to jump into a last-minute 5K.

It’s important not to go back to a completely sedentary state if you plan on racing again. “If you were to sit on the sofa [instead of easy running] and do absolutely nothing for three weeks, you would begin to detrain,” Norris adds. “It might not be that serious, but it would probably make the race not feel as good.”.

In a recent development, plus, going from the couch to another half marathon can lead to aches and pains, Norris adds. “If you go from doing nothing for three weeks to doing 13 miles, that’s a huge jump in single-session load,” she indicates, pointing to a study published in 2025 that shows jumping up your single-run volume by more than 10 percent in a 30-day span can increase injury risk.

Keeping up with a couple easy runs in between efforts will help you race your best—even when your best means having the most fun.

Kristine Kearns, a writer and avid runner, joined Runner’s World and Bicycling in July 2024. She previously coached high school girls cross country and right now competes in seasonal races, with more than six years of distance training and an affinity for weightlifting. You can find her wearing purple, baking cupcakes, and visiting her local farmers market.

#114870. Assault Fitness AssaultBike Pro X Review (2025): Assault’s Best Bike Yet?
