Industry observers note that the fund returned -7%Â¹, giving back much of last quarter's gains. Thus we are still digging out of our hole. Returns will differ by fund; please check your individual statements.

Most of what you will read in this letter comes down to one idea: the market has gotten worse at seeing. Michael Mauboussin and Dan Callahan of Morgan Stanley estimate that fundamental investors now account for only about 15% of trading volume, with much of the rest driven by quant funds and high-frequency traders. These strategies differ, but many rely on readily measurable inputs such as earnings estimates and price momentum. The information we care about often sits outside the view of many participants: in 1,000-page insurance filings, press releases that never name the customer, or hard-to-access court filings.

Sources indicate that human investors are increasingly using large language models such as ChatGPT and Claude as their first research stop. These tools allow us to cover ground rapidly, but they can also reinforce consensus. When many investors ask similar questions and start with summaries of what has already been written about a tech giant, they are likely to encounter similar explanations for what matters and what comes next. This leaves fewer investors examining the "other side of the trade." If that is happening, changes in consensus could produce more pronounced movesâa pattern consistent with my market observations.

Our portfolio is full of companies where I believe value is accruing outside the market's current focus. These dynamics may help explain why the gap between business performance and share price this year has been so wide. For several of our largest holdings, there are specific milestones over the coming quarters that should make their progress visible even to the computers, whether through reported earnings, settlements, or a sale. This letter walks through those milestones, firm by company.

Sources indicate that in the last letter, I wrote that I believed that many of our holdings were non-consensus but right, which Howard Marks and others have pointed out is the quadrant that generates the most attractive returns. At the very end of the letter, I condensed it to the following checklist:.

According to recent reports, - Lifecore (LFCR). The strategic process results in a sale or another outcome that closes the valuation gap.

In a recent development, - AnaptysBio. GSK (GSK) resolves the dispute through a settlement or acquisition.

It has been revealed that - Burford. The protein cases produce large settlements as they move through summary judgment.

According to recent reports, - Kingsway (KFS). Double-digit organic growth, accelerating EBITDA, and additional acquisitions.

Sources indicate that - Hagerty (HGTY). Operating leverage returns and results beat consensus estimates.

It has been revealed that - Cellebrite (CLBT). Genesis generates meaningful revenue and Cellebrite begins to be viewed as an AI beneficiary.

Recent findings suggest that - Compass Diversified (CODI). Assets are sold, shares are repurchased, and management is internalized.

Because the catalysts are idiosyncratic and each has its own timeline, I want to structure this letter primarily as an update on these companies and how each thesis is tracking.

In a recent development, where appropriate, I will highlight areas where it is difficult for the âmarketâ to see what is going on and how our thesis can be non-consensus and right. Seeing something before the computers only matters if there is a path to it showing up in the financials and the stock can ârerateâ as the computers see what we see.

Lifecore took a very large step toward realizing our thesis that âthe strategic process results in a sale or another outcome that closes the valuation gap.â On September 28, Lifecore revealed an agreement to be acquired at a nearly 50% premium to where the shares traded just before the announcement.

It has been revealed that in the weeks before the offer, I spent a lot of time re-underwriting Lifecore. The organization was executing operationally and winning new business, yet the share price kept drifting down. The divergence was so great (in my opinion) that I wanted to question everything.

Part of the problem is that progress is hard to see. The FDA approval process takes roughly two years, so a customer win today will likely start showing up in revenue at the end of 2028 and in earnest in 2029 as production ramps. If you look in Bloomberg for consensus 2028 or 2029 revenue or earnings numbers for Lifecore, you wonât find any. It is as if the customer wins do not exist in forward projections on Bloomberg.

It is also hard to infer progress from disclosures. Lifecoreâs customers do not want the company to announce their names, the drugs being manufactured, or expected volumes. As the graphic below indicates, Lifecore has won at least 18 programs, most announced via press release or on an earnings call, none naming the customer or contract size.

It has been revealed that the announcements do contain clues. The language is carefully chosen. A âcommercial transferâ means Lifecore is taking over manufacturing of a drug that is already approved and on the market with proven demand. Commercial transfers move faster and are more likely to become revenue. Upcoming drugs and Phase III programs are more speculative. They take longer than 24 months and still need FDA approval.

Some announcements also hint at size: âa potential top-5 customer, â â5% to 10% of capacity, â or âan eight-figure opportunity.â Together they build the foundation for a view on 2028 and 2029 even if the analysts wonât provide one.

Below is a partial example, estimating the size and probability of success of selected programs listed above.Â².

It has been revealed that laid out visually, the same exercise shows how effective upcoming management has been at selling excess capacity. We can lament the share price, but CEO Paul Josephs inherited a broken sales organization that is now working.

Industry observers note that each commercial agreement on the date it was revealed. Bubble area = estimated peak annual revenue (firm tiers); color = our conversion odds.

It has been revealed that I have attached a longer presentation with the full build for 2028 and 2029. It was very helpful in holding the position when Mr. Market had clearly given up. My bottom-up build has revenue and EBITDA compounding at 21% and 34%, respectively, and if the sales cadence continues, there is a path to a revenue CAGR above 30% and an EBITDA CAGR above 40% through 2029. Applying what I believe is a reasonable low-double-digit EBITDA multiple for a fast-growing business with extremely sticky customers, operating leverage, and contracted growth gets me to a double-digit share price.

Recent findings suggest that the current offer is $6.28 per share plus additional consideration if the firm hits certain milestones in 2028 through 2030. I have said repeatedly that I think the company is worth more than $10 per share, but even in the best-case scenario, if it hits all of the milestones, total deal consideration would be $9.67. I think there are a couple of factors at play.

One of Lifecoreâs largest shareholders is a fund run by a board member, and its most recent 13F shows the fund down to two holdings, which suggests it is winding down. That may have accelerated the sale process. In addition, the low share price is an impediment to a high offer as buyers typically don't offer a premium of more than 100% to the current share price unless there are intense competitive dynamics at play or an unwilling seller.

Industry observers note that I don't think the offer reflects fair value and we are evaluating how to vote. The deal leaves room for a superior offer. The deal is structured with a small breakup fee of $7M for a superior offer during the 30-day go-shop period and $9M for the period after the go-shop ends and before the deal closes. The deal is anticipated to close in the fourth quarter. We will see over the next two months whether another buyer agrees with our assessment and submits a higher offer.

Recent findings suggest that the shortest update belongs to AnaptysBio (ANAB), which is suing the much larger GSK. As a reminder, AnaptysBio discovered the cancer drug Jemperli and licensed it to Tesaro, which GSK bought in 2019. Part of the deal was a promise not to run cancer trials with competing drugs of the same type, and AnaptysBio claims GSK broke that promise. The restriction makes less and less sense for GSK as it spends billions building out its cancer business.

According to recent reports, GSK has tried to buy AnaptysBio multiple times. I expect GSK to either buy AnaptysBio outright or revise the royalty agreement before a final ruling, allowing GSK to gain full control of its cancer program for a fraction of what it has invested. Given the facts of the case and AnaptysBio's strong underlying economics, a 50%+ premium to our purchase price is well within my range of potential outcomes. The post-trial hearing was October 20, with a ruling expected in Q1 or Q2 2027, so we will see soon if GSK tries to buy AnaptysBio again.

Earnings estimates, one of the largest inputs for quants, are largely irrelevant here. The thesis rests on GSK's incentive to buy, and seeing that takes more than a Google search. I may be right or wrong, but I am almost certainly playing outside the view of many market participants.

Our other "legal" investment is Burford Capital (BUR). Last quarter I wrote that being right would mean "the protein cases produce large settlements as they move through summary judgment." Here is where that stands.

There are four protein cases: chicken, pork, beef, and turkey. Chicken is the largest and furthest along; what remain are the "opt-outs, " buyers who left the class-action suits because they expect to do better on their own. By our count, 23 groups of opt-outs have unresolved claims against Pilgrim's and 33 against Tyson.

Burford holds the largest unsettled claims against Pilgrim's Pride (PPC) and the second largest against Tyson. Neither firm can put chicken behind it without going to trial or settling with Burford. Both have made large payments to other opt-outs to avoid going to trial. Since 2020, Tyson has paid or reserved about $800M for chicken claims and Pilgrim's has recorded about $1.0B for chicken claims.

In a recent development, for chicken, 2027 is the key year. Summary judgment briefing finishes in March 2027 and trial is scheduled for September 2027. The larger settlements usually come after the summary judgment ruling and before the trial.

Burford will not comment on individual cases and discourages investors from trying to underwrite them: âwe always encourage investors to restrict their underwriting process to reach an investment decision to the data and inputs for the portfolio as a whole, not individual assets.â The firm is not spoon-feeding investors anything.

Recent findings suggest that we have shared some of our work on the protein cases with sell-side analysts and a legal reporter with little effect so far. Everyone grasps the soundbite that the protein cases could return more than Burfordâs market cap, but proving it means reading dockets. There is no central record of settlements and opt-out amounts are confidential. The defendants donât want to talk about the cases either.

However, one can build a bottom-up estimate of what chicken could pay. Tysonâs and Pilgrimâs filings disclose settlement expense, and PACER, bankruptcy filings, and SEC filings show who settled and when. Our estimates rely on several assumptions, so I donât want to overstate the precision, but I believe they are directionally correct.

Sources indicate that pilgrimâs pleaded guilty to price fixing and faces treble damages at trial, so it will likely settle for the most per dollar of purchases. Tysonâs cooperation with the Justice Department caps its damages at single damages, so it will logically pay less than Pilgrimâs Pride. The private producers, which admitted nothing, should settle as well. They have still paid well over $100M to the classes.

Burford holds at least $12B in qualified claims (purchaSes) from Sysco (SYY) and the bankruptcy claims of Maines Paper & Food Service. Damages experts in the case have estimated overcharges of roughly 8% to 22% depending on the period and product; a blend is about 11%, or about 33Â¢ per dollar after trebling. In theory, with treble damages, the Burford claims could be worth about $4B (about ), but the simplest way to think about the settlements is in terms of pennies on the dollar for purchases made.

Industry observers note that initial settlements in 2019â2022 were made for 1Â¢ or 2Â¢ on the dollar. As the case has progressed and trial has neared, the settlement rates seem to have gone up. In the most recent quarter, Pilgrimâs Pride settled with 13 claimants for what we estimate to be approximately 6.5Â¢ per dollar spent. There is one public data point for 8Â¢. Tyson has settled for 1Â¢ to 2Â¢ so far but may pay more as trial nears.

Our base case for settlements for just chicken in 2027 is $1.53 a share (before tax), which is material relative to Burfordâs current sub-$4 share price. The assumed settlement rates are 8Â¢ from Pilgrimâs, 4Â¢ from Tyson and 5.5Â¢ from the private producers. We have built a tool to allow you to play with the assumptions and see the status of settlements (link). The grid below reveals how gross dollar settlements translate into per share amounts.Â³.

Sources indicate that everyone is motivated to settle. Burford's debt covenants make it hard to borrow for new cases, so chicken proceeds matter to its funding, and insiders own about 9%. The defendants, except Tyson, face trebled damages at trial, which is why these cases rarely go to trial. The clock is running, and I would be surprised if the chicken claims settle for less than historical rates in 2027.

Kingsway is building a company around the search model, where it backs hungry, A-player operators, dropping them into undermanaged lifestyle businesses bought at around 5x EBITDA. As I wrote last quarter, the bogey to drive returns is "Double-digit organic growth, accelerating EBITDA, and additional acquisitions.".

On its earnings call, the company reaffirmed that it expects double-digit organic growth and 3-5 acquisitions this year. More importantly, it reported its best portfolio EBITDA in years: more than $7M for the quarter, or $28M annualized, compared to $22M over the previous 12 months.

What could this company look like in 12 months? Start with the $28M run-rate EBITDA and grow it 20% from a combination of organic growth (guided to 10% or more), acquisitions, and operating leverage, and there is a legitimate path to $33M+ of portfolio EBITDA at the end of 2027. Subtract $5M of corporate expense, apply a 20x multiple, deduct net debt ($62M) and preferred shares ($16.3M), and you get an equity value of more than $16 per share. The 20x multiple is not as rich as it sounds. The company pays effectively no taxes because of NOLs, and the businesses it owns are asset-light with minimal capex. A 20x multiple is not uncommon for growing serial acquirers, but it does imply continued organic growth and acquisitions.

Kingsway has no sell-side coverage and no earnings estimates, which makes it almost impossible for the computers to see. The steady pace of acquisitions and the GAAP accounting adjustments required for its warranty business obscure the picture further. The machines may not be looking, but the engine is working: organic growth, accelerating EBITDA, and acquisitions, driven by aligned incentives and a hungry group of A-player managers whose backgrounds include U.S. military academies, relevant work experience, and top tier MBAs. Insiders own roughly 60% of the firm, and a fresh board chair is committed to engaging the capital markets and telling the investment story.

Over the next year, organic growth, acquisitions and the divestiture of a legacy business could produce strong results and make Kingsway self-funding and GAAP profitable. That would make it attractive to a larger set of human and computer buyers.

Industry observers note that hagerty had a strong start to the year, raised full-year earnings guidance, and is making progress toward fulfilling our thesis that "operating leverage returns and results beat consensus estimates." The business is firing on all cylinders. In the first half, it added a record 279,000 fresh members, grew written premium 19% year over year, and increased cash flow from operations 91% to $186M.

The biggest fly in the ointment is a change in Hagerty's arrangement with Markel (MKL), which owns about 23% of the company. Under the revised "fronting" agreement, Hagerty makes more money (good), but GAAP accounting creates a one-year period where reported revenue declines (optically bad). The transitional charges shrink each quarter through 2026 and disappear in 2027, when year-over-year revenue comparisons will also reflect the new accounting basis in both periods. In the meantime, the transition makes apples-to-apples year-over-year GAAP comparisons incredibly difficult. The Hagerty family owns almost half the company, is managing it for the long haul, and has tried to explain the long-term benefits. The progress is temporarily hidden from the computers, but the operating metrics are industry leading.

Recent findings suggest that hagerty's quarterly earnings are hard to predict because most of them come from auto insurance, where weather can swing results from year to year. We will likely avoid any Category 4 or 5 hurricane landfall in the continental U.S. in 2026 (good for people and good for earnings). The tech giant can build and release reserves, so some of the benefit may show up in reserves rather than 2026 EPS, but it is unequivocally positive. The absence of Category 4 or 5 hurricanes and operational progress may allow accelerated earnings even in an investment year for Hagerty.

We are watching several things that few computers are tuned to: 1,000-page regulatory filings where one page matters, the number of states approving the State Farm program (now 42), online auction results for the Marketplace business (up 50% year over year), and the quiet expansion of the GEICO trial. In the meantime, I expect the organization to "beat and raise" in one or both of the next two quarters and the impact on GAAP earnings of the changes to the Markel agreement to roll off.

According to recent reports, it is too early to tell if our short-term thesis on Cellebrite is correct: "Genesis generates meaningful revenue and Cellebrite begins to be viewed as an AI beneficiary." The product debuted at the end of the second quarter, and the organization booked modest revenue and cited $1M in Genesis-related ARR. Between government procurement cycles and the many free trials Cellebrite is offering, there is not enough data on Genesis yet.

Sources indicate that on the less encouraging front, the CEO stepped down. The manufacturer called it a planned transition, but several factors, including the cut to 2026 guidance from 18% ARR growth to 16% ARR growth, make me quite skeptical of the story that it was always planned. While the CEO's departure is not a positive, all the pieces still hold. Cellebrite operates in a near-duopoly selling mission-critical software to agencies with large budgets. The agencies are labor- and talent-constrained, and Cellebrite, with its Genesis offering, provides them with an opportunity for a step-function increase in productivity from their constrained labor pool. The latest CEO is a "product" guy and is committed to building out the Cellebrite platform.

Recent findings suggest that we searched public contracts for clues on Genesis adoption. The contracts are usually too opaque to show sales by product, so that was a dead end, but they were useful for tracking federal sales. The good news is that federal procurement awards appear to be up more than 20% year over year, a clear reacceleration. Federal is under 20% of the business, so it is not a full proxy for Cellebrite's revenue, but investors have focused on it since DOGE slowed it in 2025.

Company disclosures over the next three quarters will tell us whether Genesis can boost organic growth. In the meantime, we will scour public agency procurements for evidence. We own a company with segment-leading technology, mid-teens growth, and a mid-teens P/E, with the potential to expand both.

According to recent reports, this is a newly introduced investment added last quarter. The manufacturer owns seven businesses and was built by issuing shares to buy businesses while paying management and incentive fees to an âexternalâ management company. Fraud at one of the portfolio companies, an accounting restatement, and too much debt proved too much for investors, and they fled.

Sources indicate that today, an activist is involved, one business has been sold, debt is coming down, and the restatement is behind the manufacturer. In round numbers, the shares traded at $11 at quarter end, and by my math the underlying assets are likely worth $30+ per share, but could be worth substantially more with some financial engineering. If you can sell assets, generate cash, and buy back shares at 30 cents on the dollar, the share count declines much more rapidly than the value of the remaining assets. Our thesis is âAssets are sold, shares are repurchased, and management is internalized.â.

Industry observers note that two things happened this past quarter that are encouraging. First, the incoming CEO noted, âWe are still highly committed to an additional divestiture in order to accelerate the deleveraging process... we are continuing to evaluate multiple opportunities.â He called it âan crucial part of the next stepsâ for closing the gap to intrinsic value. So management is aligned with at least part of our thesis.

In a recent development, second, several board members finally bought shares in the open market, totaling about $1.7M. Even with those purchases, the board and the external manager own a comically small portion of the firm, and in my opinion they are very vulnerable to an activist taking control. I believe the purchases show the board sees an opportunity and would like to keep its seats, which will likely require asset sales and buybacks.

In a recent development, in my view, a proxy fight will likely occur in 2027 if the divestitures do not happen under the current board. Nominations for board members are due in January. The clock is ticking; the question should be who is on the board when the divestitures and buybacks happen, not whether they happen.

Industry observers note that much of the letter has been devoted to picking through filings and building a mosaic that eventually should become visible to the computers and the market. That paradigm does not apply to KKR, the alternative manager and one of the most widely covered financial companies in the world, where nothing is hidden. Below are some metrics from its most recent quarter:.

Yet the shares are down more than 25% YTD. The metrics above are backward-looking, but many of the concerns about KKR are forward-looking. There is a lot of chatter about complications in private credit and retail investors wanting money back from semi-liquid vehicles. That is true, but also true is that the retail funds in question are less than 5% of AUM and KKR will very likely raise more private credit capital in 2026 than in any prior year. AUM is still growing.

It has been revealed that A second knock on the alternative asset managers is that they are not monetizing assets or returning capital to their limited partners, leaving those limited partners with less capital to commit to future funds. Based on recent announcements, KKR is on pace to have record monetizations this year.

The share prices of the alternative managers have moved almost in lockstep.

In my opinion, the lockstep decline is creating opportunities, because operating fundamentals and exposures to software, AI, and private credit vary by alternative manager. Even if you accept the industry headwinds as valid (I do not), we may end up owning another alternative manager with strong operating metrics and a valuation depressed by the same multiple compression.

Sources indicate that for KKR, the shares trade at approximately 13x consensus 2027 earnings. Ultimately I don't think this disconnect between fundamentals, operating performance, valuation and share price will persist. These businesses have operating leverage: as AUM goes up, earnings power goes up faster. Given the quantum of uncalled capital, fee paying AUM is going up. Unless the books are completely mismarked, earnings are going up too, and we are reaching the point where, absent a large geopolitical risk-off event, multiples should trough or even improve. A reversion to a market multiple plus continued growth would imply a return of more than 50% over the next 12 months.

As part of reducing portfolio concentration, we rebought Liquidia after it lost the patent decision. Liquidia has reached a financially manageable settlement with United Therapeutics (UTHR) that clears all legal issues between the two.

Recent findings suggest that we initiated a small newly introduced position in the AI basket. I am still not comfortable buying the first-order beneficiaries â chip manufacturers or power providers. We did, however, buy shares in Limbach, which should benefit from the unprecedented data center buildout.

Limbach designs, installs and maintains mechanical, electrical, plumbing and controls systems for commercial and institutional buildings. The core of the business is heating and air conditioning in complex facilities. Limbach bids on large, complicated projects such as hospitals and generally passes on simpler work like office buildings and warehouses. Its largest customer is the hospital operator HCA (HCA).

We owned Limbach several years ago but grew frustrated that nearly every quarter brought âone-timeâ charges that looked more routine than one-time. Back then, Limbach mostly worked as a subcontractor to general contractors. Since then, a fresh CEO has pushed the manufacturer toward work commissioned directly by building owners, and margins, profitability and predictability have all improved.

In pursuing owner-direct work, Limbach largely passed on data centers. That was costly. Data center construction now absorbs a striking share of U.S. investment, and cooling is one of the central engineering problems in those buildings. Worse, data center builders are bidding up wages for exactly the skilled labor Limbach employs, squeezing its margins without bringing any of the revenue.

It has been revealed that in the second quarter, Limbach stumbled. Gross margin fell from 28% to 21.5%, owner-direct organic revenue declined, and management cut its full-year EBITDA guidance by about 12%. The stock fell 35% the next day. Alongside the results, Limbach announced the acquisition of CYMCOR, a program manager for data center construction. The logic mirrors what Limbach did in healthcare, where its program management arm has steered roughly $60M of project work to Limbach while generating about $3M of program management fees. Limbach paid $30M, about 7.5x managementâs forecast of CYMCORâs 2027 EBITDA. The deal pays for itself only modestly on its own; the payoff comes if it opens doors to data center projects.

Sources indicate that we bought our shares at roughly 12x this yearâs free cash flow. There are credible paths to grow both revenue and margins: the business normalizing as guidance assumes, plus latest data center work. If Limbach delivers on both, the multiple will likely expand too, and we would benefit three ways.

It has been revealed that the bear case has the margin compression being permanent and the promised second-half growth not showing up. While I donât think this will happen, the shares could certainly go lower. Still, I believe the odds are skewed in our favor. The share price was more than double what we paid as recently as May, and peer multiples are nearly double Limbachâs. If Limbach is operationally successful, the share price should take care of itself.

Industry observers note that we ended the quarter short both Pilgrimâs Pride and Tyson Foods (TSN) given the potential magnitude of the settlement payments required to end their protein litigation. The companies appear to accrue for the settlement expenses as deals are signed. The potential liability is not a focus of investors as analysts rarely ask questions about the companiesâ pending litigation. Given the coming court dates, the magnitude of the settlements may surprise investors and negatively impact their share prices. We are also short a major index and a mature fast-food chain with challenged growth and a very healthy multiple.

It has been revealed that we have done the work, we have the receipts. Time will tell if we get paid. The passage of time should be our friend. This quarter, we learn whether an overbid emerges for Lifecore. In early November, Limbach reports the quarter that tests its guidance. Nominations for Compass Diversified's board are due January 21, so we will learn soon if a group emerges to push for asset sales and buybacks. The AnaptysBio ruling should arrive in the first half of 2027. Over the next two quarters, the Markel accounting noise rolls off and Hagerty's GAAP numbers become useful again. Over the next three quarters, Cellebrite's traction with its Genesis product and ability to sustain growth will become clear. By the end of March, summary judgment briefing in chicken is complete, with a September 2027 trial pushing the chicken defendants toward settlement and bringing cash to Burford.

In a recent development, we will know if we are right or not; there will be results for the computers to see or not. Non-consensus will become consensus or not. Multiples can compress or expand. That is out of our control, but we know what we own and why we own it and look forward to the computers seeing what we see.

#114743. $656,000 of Frugal Things I Still Love Doing

📅 24 Jul 2024 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1993 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mrmoneymustache ↗ Open Full Page

$656,000 of Frugal Things I Still Love Doing

📅 24 Jul 2024 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1993 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that “I used to read Mr.
  • “Until he got all rich and fancy so that he no longer understands the common person’s plight.
  • Stash probably doesn’t even practice any of these money-saving things he preaches any more!”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that “I used to read Mr. Money Mustache”,.

“Until he got all rich and fancy so that he no longer understands the common person’s plight.

Stash probably doesn’t even practice any of these money-saving things he preaches any more!”.

When I read things like this, I can’t help but laugh. Because on the one hand, when you put a bunch of personal life details online like this, being misunderstood is just part of the package. But on the other hand, if the critics could peek in and see our real lives – not just mine but those of all the Mustachians – they would have to give up their conspiracy theories and accept the fact that this stuff just works.

In a recent development, because really, not much has changed when it comes to the basics. Like many MMM readers over the past twelve years, my total wealth level has increased pretty regularly. But also like many of us, I haven’t felt the need to change very much about my spending because I was doing my best to live an enjoyable life in the first place.

How have so many people found such great success? I think we Mustachians have something that’s a bit more rare and special than standard financial advice, which is what makes it work so well:.

In a recent development, standard Advice: Slash your spending and make sacrifices until you reach a certain savings percentage, and beyond that it doesn’t matter, it’s all personal choice. More income? Great, that means you don’t have to sacrifice as much! FatFIRE for everyone!

It has been revealed that mustachianism: Cultivate a love of efficiency, creativity, self awareness, and self improvement. Use this knowledge to improve your life in all ways, including those which help you live better even as your monthly expense rate drops over time.

So what does this mean in practice?

Sources indicate that well, I’ll give you some examples from my own present-day life. Things I do because I happen to enjoy them, which also happen to save a lot of money. Some of these are normal, some are silly and may end up in some future gossip magazine hit piece, but all of them happen to work for me, so the critics can be damned.

As I list each item, I’ll include an estimate of how much the activity saves me per decade, because you should always think at least in terms of decades. To make that calculation yourself, just use the “rule of 172” – take a monthly expense and multiply it by 172 to estimate how much it would compound into over ten years, if invested.

1) Fixing my own House (and everybody else’s too).

In a recent development, I’m a big believer in self-sufficiency, and working to build up the skills to manage the most important parts of your own life without depending on too many things (or people) that are outside of your control. In other words, one giant recipe for a happy life is simply to Become a Producer of the Things You Most Enjoy Consuming.

And in my case, I happen to love houses. I like living in beautiful, functional spaces and sharing them with friends. But most houses are ugly and poorly designed when you buy them, so I realized that I also love solving problems and redesigning old buildings to become latest again. I enjoy this process so much that I spend most of my free time doing it – on both my own properties and the homes of friends.

According to recent reports, and I love teaching other people to gain power over their own houses too. It’s amazing how great people feel as they lose their fear and dependence on outside contractors, and gain the ability to fix and maintain things with their own two hands.

Savings: An average of $20,000 per year = $287,000 per decade.

You know what’s great? Having so much money that you can buy whatever you want – high quality things which get delivered to your front door the very next day.

Recent findings suggest that you know what’s even better? Not buying some of those new things, and instead finding ways to share, repurpose and buy equally high quality items from other people who don’t need them any more. All while building up your own community and creating new friendships in the process.

Sources indicate that craigslist, Facebook Marketplace, and even NextDoor all have Buy Nothing groups for most areas. In the MMM-HQ community, we run a Discord server with about 200 local people, who chat around the clock on a wide range of subjects. They help each other with major projects in one channel called #diyhowto, and give away and sell things on #forsale and #buynothing.

Although our private Discord group is my favorite, I also use Craigslist regularly, and probably save (and earn) a few thousand every year thanks to the habit:.

Savings: About $42,000 per decade.

Recent findings suggest that we all know that Mr. Money Mustache’s biggest contribution to personal finance is to insist that bike transportation is the best way to get around. And I still feel this way. As we learned in The True Cost of Commuting, cars cost at least 50 cents per mile to operate, while bikes are much cheaper, mainly due to reduced depreciation and maintenance costs (which are even bigger than the gas savings).

Industry observers note that I do still use bikes (or walking) for at least 95% of my local trips these days, but because I live in the center of a small city, my life is pretty local. So this still only adds up to about 2000 miles per year, a savings of “only” $14,000 per decade.

In a recent development, but when you choose active transportation, there’s much more to the picture than just cutting your car expenses. You’re changing everything about your physical and mental health picture for the better, which brings us to the next point of….

In a recent development, although I’m no competitive athlete, whenever I see an option to make my body work a bit harder, I usually take it. Stairs instead of elevators, running the golf course instead of using a golf cart, moving my own furniture and appliances instead of calling a mover, shoveling snow and raking leaves instead of using a machine.

According to recent reports, when I face a decision like this, I simply ask myself the question: “Well, Mustache. Do you want MORE health and fitness, or LESS?” Putting it in that context makes the answer obvious. Every bit helps, because when it comes to your body, the rule is pretty much use it or lose it.

It has been revealed that but how much money does this save? There’s no real way to calculate it exactly, but I like to think of it this way: The US average health care spending is about $13,000 per person per year. My lifetime costs due to illness or medication so far have been just about zero, plus I know I’ve had more energy and greater productivity due to being healthy. Let’s just put it very conservatively and set the estimated savings and benefits at $10k per year which means.

Estimated Savings:  $140,000 per decade.

5) Saving Energy by Running my home like a Glamping Retreat.

Here’s where things get a bit silly, but my level of joy is actually at its greatest.

In a recent development, my personality type is probably a weird combination of an engineer, a carpenter, an artsy hippie, and a mad scientist. Oh, and a devoted homebody too. Because of this, my favorite activity most days is to just run around my house taking care of things and trying new little experiments and improvements.

Industry observers note that sometimes I’ll cut a few significant holes on on the South side of the house and install sliding doors and big windows to allow nice sunbeams and passive solar energy to get into my house and give me free heat in the winters. Other times it’s just smaller things to save energy and live more at at one with the seasons of my area:.

Even taken all together, these things are pretty small – the average combined gas and electric bill for my area is about $250 per month, while my usage adds up to about $75. So while we’re only saving about $30,000 per decade for what sounds like a lot of work to most people, I consider this to be the biggest win because I enjoy living in “MMM’s Energy Efficiency Playground” so much.

6) Local Living over Constant Travel.

“Hey, we’re having a major back yard pool party next weekend to celebrate Amy’s graduation from kindergarten, can you make it?”.

Industry observers note that “OH NOOOO!!! We will be off in at Disneyland that whole week! We planned the trip months ago, I wish we could make it!

As I type this in the height of the summer season, I really feel this effect at its fullest: almost all of my friends are off on trips, and my guest suite here at home is almost constantly full. People are traveling a lot, and many of them sound like they wish they could spend a few more of their precious summer weeks and weekends at home.

Industry observers note that I’ll let you in on a little secret: you can! The trick is saying, “no thanks” more often to looks that involve you being away, and “yes please” to things that let you stay at home. The benefits are numerous:.

Estimated Savings: Even if you replace just two weeks of travel for a family of four, with equivalent time at home you might save $5,000 per year in direct costs and a further $5,000 per year in incidental benefits like the health and local friendships. This would work out to a shocking $143,000 per decade of wealth increase!

According to recent reports, of course, travel is generally a good thing for broadening the life experience of you and your kids. It’s worth spending on, lavishly at times. But the key is to balance it out and be discerning, keeping the most enriching trips and pruning a few off the bottom of the list. And remembering that home time is valuable and healthy too.

And Whoa! We’ve already built up a huge list and I feel like I was just getting started.

Taken all together, we’ve already detailed things that compound to $656,000 every decade, which already more than double the median wealth that most American seniors have as they cruise nervously into their retirement years – after over 40 years of work!

And now that I’ve been writing this blog for over ten years myself, I can safely say that over $656,000 of even my most recent worth increases are directly attributable to these simple habits. The same ones many of us have been enjoying and preaching about all along, both before and after our retirement dates.

In a recent development, if money is in genuinely short supply, you could go a lot further than the examples in this article. And indeed, there’s a lot more laid out in this blog or the MMM Boot Camp email series.

But one of the points of Mustachianism is that you usually don’t have to try all that hard. Just tweaking your lifestyle to be slightly less ridiculous and more efficient than average is usually all it takes.

In the comments: what are your quirks and frugal indulgences? The things you do now to save money, or things you still do even after it’s no longer about the money? I often wonder how widespread this frugality-just-for-fun is. But since we Humans are a naturally curious and problem solving species in our natural state, I suspect there are many more of us out there.

JAL Business Class via Multiple Transfer Partners

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3292 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Choosefi

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • World-class Japanese hospitality at a fraction of the cash price via partner bookings.
  • Recent findings suggest that picture this: you're settled into your own private suite at 37,000 feet somewhere over the Pacific.
  • The core insight here is deceptively simple: JAL's own frequent flyer program is not where you want to book this award.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

World-class Japanese hospitality at a fraction of the cash price via partner bookings.

Fuel Surcharges via Partner Programs.

Recent findings suggest that picture this: you're settled into your own private suite at 37,000 feet somewhere over the Pacific. The door closes. A flight attendant in a crisp JAL uniform offers you a warm towel and asks how you'd like your appetizer served. The flat bed is already made with a proper duvet. Outside the window, the sun is setting over the ocean. You're nine hours into a 12-hour flight to Tokyo, and you feel more rested than you did when you boarded. This is JAL's Sky Suite — one of the most celebrated business class products in the world — and with the right travel rewards strategy, your family can experience it for a fraction of what everyone else is paying. Here's the math that stops people cold: a round-trip business class ticket from San Francisco to Tokyo on JAL typically retails for **$5,000 to $10,000 per person**. That's not a typo. Premium transcontinental fares are genuinely that expensive, and most people simply accept that they'll never sit up front on a 12-hour flight across the Pacific. But the ChooseFI community knows better. That same seat — the same flat bed, the same Champagne, the same Sky Suite cocoon — is available for **60,000 miles** when booked through Alaska Mileage Plan or American AAdvantage. At a retail value of $5,000 to $10,000, you're looking at **8.3 to 16.7 cents per point** in value. For context, most travel rewards experts consider anything above 1.5 cents per point a good redemption. This one can be up to *eleven times* that benchmark. The pricing inefficiency exists because partner award programs — like Alaska and American — use fixed award charts that were negotiated years ago, before JAL's hard product became one of the most sought-after cabins in the sky. JAL hasn't raised these partner pricing levels proportionally as cash fares have climbed. The gap between what you pay in points and what the market charges in dollars is enormous, and it's yours to exploit right now. This isn't a loophole that's about to close tomorrow. It's a structural feature of the loyalty system — one that rewards people who understand how to use their points strategically rather than burning them on domestic economy upgrades. For anyone on the path to financial independence, where every dollar and every point is treated with intention, this is exactly the kind of asymmetric opportunity worth understanding.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: JAL's own frequent flyer program is not where you want to book this award. This is the aha moment that separates casual points users from strategic ones.

JAL operates its own loyalty program — JAL Mileage Bank — but it charges significant fuel surcharges on its own award tickets, often running $100 to $500 or more per ticket. When you book JAL business class through JAL Mileage Bank itself, those surcharges erode a substantial portion of your points value before you even leave the ground. The ChooseFI community's editorial guidance here is unambiguous: book JAL through partner programs to avoid this tax on your redemption.

There are two primary programs where you can book JAL business class at 60,000 miles round-trip on the transpacific route:.

Sources indicate that alaska Mileage Proposal prices JAL business class at 60,000 miles for a round-trip between North America and Japan. Alaska is a oneworld partner of JAL and honors JAL's genuinely strong award availability. Critically, Alaska does not pass through JAL's fuel surcharges to awards booked through Mileage Plan. This is a massive advantage.

American AAdvantage also prices the same route at 60,000 miles round-trip. Both programs use fixed award charts, meaning the price doesn't fluctuate with demand the way cash fares do — a $10,000 ticket at peak cherry blossom season costs exactly the same points as a ticket in a slower travel month.

Neither Alaska Mileage Proposal nor American AAdvantage is a direct transfer partner from the major US bank programs in the same way Chase or Amex partners work. However, you have real pathways:.

For Alaska and American miles specifically, the strongest earning strategies involve:.

Both Alaska and American use fixed award charts — meaning the price in miles is the same regardless of how high the cash price climbs. This is the structural inefficiency at work. A seat that retails for $10,000 during peak season still costs 60,000 miles. The chart doesn't care about demand; it just prices by region and cabin. As long as JAL releases availability — and they do — the gap between cash cost and points cost remains enormous.

JAL also allows one free stopover and one open jaw per round-trip award, which means you can potentially add a stop in Tokyo itself while continuing to another Japanese city, or fly into one city and out of another — all at no additional miles cost.

It has been revealed that this is the cardinal rule of all travel rewards bookings: never transfer points until you have confirmed availability. Points transfers are generally irreversible.

Industry observers note that go to ba.com (British Airways Executive Club) to search for JAL award availability. Because BA is also a oneworld partner, their search tool reveals you JAL award space. Let's run the numbers on a specific scenario that thousands of ChooseFI members have used as a benchmark: San Francisco (SFO) to Tokyo Narita (NRT) in JAL business class, round-trip for two people.

#114726. Breaking: Six Dumb Misconceptions About The Economy (that the Politicians Want You To Believe)

Breaking: Six Dumb Misconceptions About The Economy (that the Politicians Want You To Believe)

📅 13 Oct 2024 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2001 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Well, it looks like we’re here in another US election year already.
  • Industry observers note that as Advanced Mustachians, we already know that the ongoing battle of Harris vs.
  • In a recent development, but out of all the things the politicians like to bicker about, there’s one area where MMM does need to set the record straight, and that area is of course money.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Well, it looks like we’re here in another US election year already.

Industry observers note that as Advanced Mustachians, we already know that the ongoing battle of Harris vs. Trump should not be consuming much of our time. Sure, we do our research and cast our votes but after that we move right on to focus on other things within our own circle of control.

In a recent development, but out of all the things the politicians like to bicker about, there’s one area where MMM does need to set the record straight, and that area is of course money. Your money, the economy in general, and the overall wealth of the nation.

Recent findings suggest that politicians are already not known for being the sharpest tools in the shed when it comes to technical stuff like science, technology, or economics. But this year the discourse has become particularly dumb, as our candidates try to manipulate undecided voters in swing states with ideas that are based on irrational emotions rather than sound economic sense.

For one particularly funny example, you may have noticed that the competing party (Trump in this case) is attacking the incumbents (Biden/Harris) over the “bad economy.” When in fact the US economy is stronger than it has ever been, with the lowest unemployment we’ve ever seen as well.

It’s hard to imagine a better situation than we have right now, and in fact the recent bout of higher inflation is a sign that things have been going too well, and we needed to step on the brakes with the help of higher interest rates.

But somehow the people still seem to believe that we have a “bad” economy. Take a look at this Gallup poll showing that while most people (85%) are doing really well right now, they assume that it’s just their own good fortune – only 17% believe the economy is doing well.

Sources indicate that this is mathematically impossible, because if most people are doing well, that’s the definition of a good economy! And suspiciously enough, this widespread wrongness correlates quite nicely with the rise of social media misinformation.

So the politicians and the news have been doing the opposite of what they should be doing in an ideal situation (sharing accurate information). And sure, we can always just ignore their speeches and go on with our lives. But when it comes to economics, knowledge is power (and money). The more accurately we understand how things really work, the wealthier we will all become.

So with all that in mind, I hereby present you with my list of the….

Top Dumb Things Politicians Want You To Believe About The Economy.

1: The President Controls the Economy.

If there’s a recession, the opposition party likes to blame it on the current president. If the economy is booming, the current president likes to give himself (or possibly soon herself) credit for all of that success. But really, the US economy is way too significant – and thankfully way too free – for the president to control or really even influence all that strongly.

Recent findings suggest that in reality, our economy is a gigantic machine which converts labor and materials into things like iPhones, hospitals and pumpkin pies. And although we’re the biggest economy at 26% of the planet, we are still heavily influenced by that much bigger 74% of economic activity that the other 7.6 billion people on Earth are busy producing everywhere else.

When we have our inevitable little boom and bust cycles, they are mostly caused by the normal cycle of irrational exuberance (and greed) like the 2007 housing boom, followed by brief periods of extreme fear and pessimism like the 2008-2012 financial and housing crash.

In a recent development, the government does play a role too, by setting tax rates and other rules. But the effects of these policies are usually so delayed and unpredictable, that you can’t draw a straight line between today’s president and today’s economy. In other words, the government does its best to adjust the rudder on our giant ship, but in the short term our economy lurches around on the waves and storms of the ocean.

2: The President Controls Interest Rates.

This one is especially funny to me, as our candidates feign sympathy for the hard life of middle class Americans, who now face higher borrowing costs on their credit cards and car loans and mortgages. They claim they will fight to bring the interest rates down. Trump even goes as far as bullying our Federal Reserve board members (who can only do their jobs if we allow them to function as independent experts) and suggesting that he would take over the whole department, if elected.

The real story is that while monetary policy would be a terrible tool to leave in the hands of a sitting president (see Argentina), it does function as an excellent set of gas and brake pedals for the economy if used properly. When things slow down and unemployment gets too high, a cut to the interest rates will produce a boost in everything from new jobs to stock prices. But if things get too hot, you get rapid inflation which can mess up the system.

3: Inflation has Made Life Harder for Americans (and the President Can Magically Reverse it).

Sources indicate that this line of reasoning is even dumber than the last one. For a couple of years after the Covid era, we had rapid inflation. It was caused by a rare combination of a goods shortage caused by things like factory closures and remote work, plentiful demand from government stimulus spending and low interest rates. These factors have since ironed themselves out, and inflation is back down to an ultra-low 2.4%.

But most significantly, wages have still risen faster than inflation so we are all better off than before! Since 2019, overall prices are up 19% and our wages are up 21%. So even after all that inflation, we are still doing just fine. But the candidates are still bickering over inflation as if it’s an actual problem, and even worse promising to “bring prices back down”. And they’ve managed to convince the electorate that “higher wages and prices” is the same thing as “a bad economy”. Which is just plain wrong.

According to recent reports, bonus dumbness: politicians also occasionally blame “greedy corporations” for increasing prices to hoard profits. While price increases are totally acceptable in a market system (as a business owner you are free to set prices wherever you like), in reality it doesn’t usually happen because our markets are too competitive. For example, a recent deep analysis from NPR showed that no, grocery stores haven’t made any windfall profit at all off of this recent bout of Covid-fueled inflation.

4: The President Controls Housing Prices.

Industry observers note that one vital thing that has changed over the past ten years is that US house prices and rents have both risen much faster than general inflation and even wages. On the positive side, interest rates have also risen which tends to make houses feel more expensive and is supposed to help bring house prices down. But it hasn’t happened yet which means we have the double whammy of higher prices and higher interest costs for mortgage borrowers.

Sources indicate that the dumb part is that our candidates are proposing things that would make the problem even worse, like subsidies for first-time homebuyers or schemes to reduce the interest rates. When really the solution is to increase the supply of housing, which I personally think will happen if we stop putting up roadblocks for homebuilders (myself included) to build housing.

Things like faster and cheaper permits, less onerous and expensive building codes, eliminating suburban-style zoning and setback and car parking rules, and changing laws so that NIMBYs no longer get any say over what other people do with their own land could all help reduce the cost of building a house by about 50%, quickly and permanently.

5: The President Controls Gas Prices, and They Are Right now “High” and We Want Them Lower.

Ahh, gasoline! The most ridiculous of things to worry about and the fuel for many of MMM’s rants since 2011.

First of all, on an inflation-adjusted basis, gasoline is still about the same price as it was in 1950: in the $3-4 range per gallon, in today’s dollars.

Secondly, it is so cheap that even with our huge inefficient American vehicles, the average household is still only spending 2.5% of their disposable income on the stuff! (The funny part is that they spend many times more on the rest of the car ownership experience while thinking gas is the part that is expensive).

Sources indicate that third, gasoline has been obsolete for almost a decade now. You can get a used electric car for less than the price of a comparable used gas car, or if you’re a fancypants money waster like me, new EVs are also cheaper than their gas counterparts. You get a faster, nicer car that almost never needs maintenance OR gasoline, and save money.

So why are we even still talking about this antique fuel of a previous era? Why aren’t the candidates also arguing over the price of Kodak film or typewriters or fax machines?

6: The Economy is Something We Should Even Worry About.

In a recent development, the funniest part about all this economic talk is that we’re focusing on the wrong thing. While hard work and business and advancing the frontiers of human knowledge are all fun things, the reality is that we passed the point of having “Enough” decades ago. When the American middle class complains about how hard we have it these days, it’s like a bunch of overfed people at a buffet wishing they could just have one more flavor of donuts stacked onto the table.

In a recent development, yes, we have income and wealth inequality so that the rich tend to get richer more swiftly. And yes, we should keep that in check with a somewhat progressive tax system because a more equal society tends to be a more peaceful and happy one.

But have you noticed that as the rich people get richer, they don’t get any happier? It’s because after you pass the point of “Enough”, adding more money doesn’t really help much.

Sources indicate that and “Enough” is much more defined by your mindset (and your collection of life skills) than your paycheck. So if the politicians really cared about improving our happiness and wellbeing, they’d be preaching the Principles of Mustachianism rather than pandering to the specific requests of coal miners or billionaires.

It has been revealed that but alas, winning an election is a very different thing than proposing stuff that is actually best for the country. And for that reason, we cast our votes for the best party and then tune back out until the next election.

In the Comments: Has the election season been getting you down, pumping you up, or just giving you a thorough dose of “Meh”?

While researching economic stats for this article, I came across a quirky but informative series of videos called USA Facts by none other than former Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer. It seems that he had the same frustration as me: Americans are fighting over a bunch of opinions and misinformation without even bothering to look up the actual facts. So he made a well-produced series of videos that just share the facts without the baggage of political hype on top of them. I wish our politicians could do the same thing!

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

A recurring monthly opportunity to book premium cabin flights at economy-level points pricing.

Typical Promo Biz Class One-Way.

Fuel Surcharges on Promo Awards.

Picture this: you're reclining in Air France's La Première-adjacent Business cabin somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of Champagne in hand, a three-course meal on the way, and a fully flat bed waiting for you after dinner. The couple in economy paid $900 for this flight. You paid 40,000 Flying Blue miles — points you transferred from your Chase Sapphire Reserve in seconds — and the cash value of what you're sitting in is closer to $2,500 to $6,000. That gap is the entire point. Air France-KLM's Flying Blue program runs what they call **Promo Rewards** — a monthly flash sale on award seats that slashes the points price by 25 to 50% on select routes. In Business class, that can mean seats that would normally cost 80,000+ miles dropping to as low as 40,000 miles one-way. On a route where a cash ticket retails for $3,000, you're extracting **7.5 cents per point** — and on premium routes during peak travel periods, that figure can climb to 15 cents per point. To put that in FI-community terms: the average point is worth 1 to 2 cents when redeemed for cash back or basic travel. This redemption can be worth 6 to 10 times that. If you have 40,000 transferable points sitting in a Chase or Amex account, this is the difference between a $400 economy ticket and a $3,000 business class experience — for the same points. The pricing inefficiency exists because Flying Blue uses these promotional awards as a marketing tool to fill premium cabin seats on specific dates that might otherwise go out with empty seats. Airlines would rather have a loyalist in that seat than fly it empty. You, as someone who's built a transferable points balance, are perfectly positioned to take advantage of the moment they make that trade-off. This isn't a loophole that's about to close. Flying Blue has run Promo Rewards consistently for years. It's a **structural feature of the program** — one the ChooseFI community can build an annual travel strategy around. The challenge isn't finding the deal. It's being ready when it drops.

The mechanism behind Flying Blue Promo Rewards is elegantly simple once you understand it, and it separates this program from virtually every other airline loyalty play in your toolkit.

Flying Blue Has a Dynamic Award Chart — With a Monthly Override.

According to recent reports, flying Blue moved to dynamic pricing, which typically means the program is less predictable and often less valuable than the old fixed-chart days. But here's where it gets interesting: Promo Rewards operate as a fixed-price overlay on top of that dynamic system. On the 1st of each month (or within the first few days), Flying Blue publishes a curated list of routes — often 20 to 40 city pairs — with fixed, deeply discounted mile prices. Business class seats on transatlantic routes regularly appear at 40,000 to 50,000 miles one-way. These are not dynamic prices that will creep up as demand increases. They're locked promotional rates on specific routes.

This means the program essentially gives you two separate games to play: the chaotic dynamic pricing game (usually skip it), and the monthly Promo Rewards game (always pay attention).

The Fuel Surcharge Nuance You Must Know.

Flying Blue does pass on carrier-imposed surcharges for standard awards on Air France and KLM flights — this can add $200 to $500 to what should be a points redemption. But here's the critical detail: Promo Reward bookings eliminate those surcharges. You pay the miles, a small booking fee, and that's it. This is a significant hidden value that casual points users miss entirely. The published cash price comparison becomes even more favorable once you factor in that you're not paying the surcharge on top.

The Transfer Path Is Best-in-Class.

Flying Blue partners with every major transferable currency at a 1:1 ratio:.

The instant transfer speeds from Chase, Amex, and Citi are critical here. When Promo Rewards drop and the best dates start disappearing within hours, you cannot afford a 3-day transfer window. If your points are in Chase or Amex, you can see a seat, transfer, and book in under 10 minutes.

Routing Rules Give You Flexibility.

Flying Blue allows open-jaw routing — meaning you can fly into Paris and out of Amsterdam (or vice versa) on a single award, letting you proposal a more dynamic European itinerary without paying for two separate tickets. The booking window opens at 359 days out, and miles are activity-based with a 24-month expiration window, so you're not racing against a clock as long as you keep your account active with occasional small transactions.

It has been revealed that before the 1st of any month arrives, you need to be ready. Create a free Flying Blue account at flyingblue.com if you don't have one. More importantly, ensure your transferable points — Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, Citi ThankYou, Capital One, or Bilt — are linked and ready. Don't transfer anything yet. You want to see the actual Promo Reward routes before moving a single point.

Recent findings suggest that when the list drops, you'll see a curated set of origin/destination city pairs with fixed Business class prices. Look for transatlantic routes from major U.S. gateways (New York, Los Angeles, Atlanta, Chicago, Miami) to European hubs like Paris (CDG) or Amsterdam (AMS).

Go to flyingblue.com and use the award search tool. Enter your origin and destination from the Promo list. Switch the cabin to Business. Search across a 30-day window if possible — the calendar view shows you which dates have availability. Act within hours, not days. The best dates — particularly weekends, school holidays, and summer dates — disappear fast.

Note: Flying Blue's search only shows Air France and KLM metal for Promo Rewards. SkyTeam partner availability is separate and won't be Promo-priced.

It has been revealed that do not transfer points yet. Confirm the exact flights, dates, and total miles cost. Take a screenshot. Note the flight numbers and times. Availability can disappear between the moment you see it and the moment you book, so move promptly through the next steps.

From your bank portal (Chase, Amex, Citi), initiate the transfer to Flying Blue. For Chase, Amex, and Citi, transfers are instant. Capital One and Bilt take 1–2 days, so these are less ideal for Promo Rewards' speed-dependent window. Transfer exactly what you need — Promo award prices are fixed, so there's no cushion math required.

In a recent development, with miles in your account, return to the award search, re-confirm your dates are still available, and book. You'll pay the fixed Promo miles price plus taxes and fees (minimal, with no fuel surcharges on Promo awards). You'll receive a confirmation email immediately.

Don't panic. Wait for next month. Or search the current month's Promo list for alternative routes — sometimes less popular city pairs have excellent availability. You can also check if the same route appears at standard dynamic pricing, but compare the CPP carefully before transferring for a non-Promo redemption.

Flying Blue moved to dynamic award pricing, which normally makes costs unpredictable and often unfavorable. But the Promo Rewards program creates a monthly fixed-price override on select routes that dramatically undercuts the dynamic system. Each month, Flying Blue publishes a curated list of discounted routes with pricing 25 to 50 percent below standard and with fuel surcharges eliminated entirely. This creates a repeatable, predictable opportunity cycle: check on the 1st, find a discounted route, transfer points instantly from Chase or Amex, and book before the best dates are taken. The structural advantage is that most casual travelers do not know about Promo Rewards or do not act fast enough — which leaves more availability for prepared ChooseFI community members who treat the 1st of each month as a mini-booking event.

Do This: Set a Monthly Calendar Reminder for the 1st.

Sources indicate that flying Blue Promo Rewards are time-sensitive by design. The best routes with the best dates are gone within 24–48 hours of announcement. Put a recurring reminder on your calendar. Treat the 1st of each month like a mini-event.

Do This: Keep a Points Buffer in Your Transferable Accounts.

Because Promo Rewards require fast action and the best transfer partners (Chase, Amex, Citi) are instant, you want at least 40,000–80,000 points already sitting in your transferable account before the announcement. Don't be in a position where you need to wait on a credit card statement to close before you can transfer.

Do This: Use Open-Jaw Routing to Maximize Your Trip.

In a recent development, flying Blue allows open-jaw routing. Book into Paris (CDG) and out of Amsterdam (AMS) — or any combination of Air France/KLM hub cities — and you've just built a multi-country European trip into a single award booking. This is the kind of routing flexibility that turns a one-city trip into a proper adventure.

Do This: Track Multiple Months of Route Patterns.

Recent findings suggest that promo routes rotate monthly, but certain routes appear repeatedly — particularly transatlantic and routes between European hubs and Africa or the Middle East. After 2–3 months of observation, you'll start to recognize patterns and can blueprint your travel around routes that are likely to repeat.

Avoid This: Transferring Points Before Confirming Availability.

In a recent development, this is the single biggest mistake beginners make. Always confirm the specific flight, date, and cabin availability before transferring points. Miles are a one-way street — you cannot transfer them back. If availability disappears after you've transferred, you're left with Flying Blue miles that may not be useful for your target route at standard (non-Promo) pricing.

Avoid This: Ignoring Standard Award Pricing.

Recent findings suggest that flying Blue's dynamic pricing outside of Promo Rewards can be punishingly expensive. A Business class seat that costs 40,000 Promo miles might cost 90,000+ miles at standard dynamic pricing. Always wait for the Promo if you can — patience pays.

Industry observers note that the ideal earning setup for this redemption combines a Chase Sapphire Reserve (3x on travel and dining, instant transfer to Flying Blue) with an Amex Gold or Platinum (4x on dining/groceries or 5x on flights respectively, also instant transfer). Between two cards, you can accumulate 40,000–80,000 points in a single year of normal household spending.

Best For: Flexible Couples and Solo Travelers Who Plan in Advance.

This redemption is purpose-built for the FI community member who thinks in systems, not spontaneous splurges. You're someone who has already built a transferable points balance of at least 40,000–80,000 points across Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, or Citi ThankYou — and who can act decisively when the right route appears.

Sources indicate that couples are the sweet spot. Two people, two Business class seats, one incredible transatlantic experience. Solo travelers benefit enormously too — a single seat at 40,000 miles is one of the highest-CPP solo redemptions in the entire transferable points ecosystem.

6 Best Subscription Management Apps (To Cancel Recurring Transactions)

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Managing your money isn’t just about earning more.
  • Before choosing an app, know what features matter most:.
  • In a recent development, rocket Money is one of the most well-known subscription managers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Managing your money isn’t just about earning more. It’s also about stopping unnecessary losses. In today’s digital economy, recurring subscription charges (streaming services, premium apps, trials, memberships) quietly drain money each month. Most people spend hundreds, or even thousands, annually on services they don’t use. Subscription manager apps help you see recurring charges, track billing cycles, and cancel those you no longer want.

Before choosing an app, know what features matter most:.

In a recent development, rocket Money is one of the most well-known subscription managers. It scans your linked bank and credit accounts for recurring charges and displays them on a clear dashboard. People like it for its ability to detect subscriptions and assist with cancellations directly in the app, a major time-saver for busy people.

Why it stands out• Automatically detects recurring payments• Lets you cancel unwanted subscriptions directly from the app• Includes extra budgeting tools and spending alerts• Trusted security with read-only bank access.

Who it’s for: People who want the fastest way to spot and stop unwanted recurring charges without manually entering every service.

Sources indicate that trim is another financial assistant that scans transactions and flags recurring charges. While subscription tracking is a smaller part of its feature set, it also provides bill negotiation support and money-saving alerts. Many owners like Trim because it reaches out on your behalf about subscriptions via text or in-app messaging.

Why it stands out• Recurring transaction detection• Alerts about unusual subscriptions or trials converting to paid• Bill negotiation tools beyond basic subscription tracking.

Who it’s for: People who want automation plus help reducing bills and optimizing spending.

PocketGuard is primarily a budgeting app that includes subscription tracking as part of a broader financial overview. Instead of being solely a subscription manager, it integrates recurring expenses into your overall budget, helping you get a full picture of your finances.

Why it stands out• Syncs automatically with financial accounts• Highlights recurring expenses in the context of your whole budget• Helps track cash flow and affordability.

Who it’s for: People who want subscriptions tracked inside a complete personal finance dashboard.

Industry observers note that monarch Money offers robust financial planning tools: budgets, goals, net worth tracking, and more, with subscription visibility included in the package. Owners often choose it for its highly customizable interface and deep analytics. It’s not subscription-only, but it gives you full clarity on recurring expenses as part of larger planning.

Why it stands out• Powerful budgeting + subscription tracking.• Clean, customizable data visuals.• Goal-based money management.

Who it’s for: Users who want subscription insights in the context of total financial planning — and who are okay paying for premium features.

Recent findings suggest that if you don’t want to link bank accounts, Bobby is a lightweight subscription tracker that lets you manually enter each subscription, along with billing dates and amounts. It then sends reminders so you don’t forget renewals. It’s simple, privacy-friendly, and great for a hands-on approach.

Why it stands out• No bank/credit card linking required.• Clean and minimal interface.• Calendar views and notification reminders.

Who it’s for: Privacy-focused users or those who prefer full manual control.

In a recent development, subby offers functionality similar to Bobby’s but is known for integrations and subscription reminders tailored for Android owners. It lets you manually track expenses with flexible billing schedules and alerts. (While not all resources list Subby as a top pick, it’s frequently mentioned among good manual trackers.).

Why it stands out• Manual entry with customizable notifications.• Good choice for Android users.

Who it’s for: People who want a simple manual tracker without linking financial accounts.

If you’d rather not use a third-party app at all, both Apple and Google offer direct subscription management:.

iPhone (Apple Subscriptions):Settings → Your Name → Subscriptions → Select subscription → Cancel Subscription.

Android (Google Play):Open Google Play → Subscriptions → Select subscription → Cancel subscription.

These built-in tools won’t automatically find all recurring charges if some are billed outside the app stores, but they are a secure and effective way to manage many mobile subscriptions.

Here’s a quick guide based on what matters most to you:.

You can also combine approaches — use a subscription app plus your budgeting system to spot recurring leaks and proposal better for annual vs monthly charges.

Subscription manager apps help plug the leaks in your financial bucket, so more of your hard-earned money stays where it belongs: with you. Whether you want automatic detection and help with cancellations, a full financial overview, or full privacy with manual entry, there’s an option that fits your style. Explore one or two subscription manager apps that align with your priorities, and don’t forget to check your finances regularly.
